React Utilities

react Overview ​

What It Is ​

blendsdk/react is the React application layer of BlendSDK. It supplies the cross-cutting infrastructure of a BlendSDK single-page application — session-based authentication against an OIDC backend-for-frontend (BFF), declarative role and permission checks, asynchronous internationalization, and a global loading overlay — as a small set of context providers, guard components, and hooks. It also provides useObjectState, a local-state utility for object-shaped component state. The package is not a visual component library: apart from the loader overlay it renders no styled UI, leaving presentation to the application or its design system. It targets React 19, is written in strict TypeScript, ships declaration files, and exposes its entire public surface from a single ESM entry point.

FactValue
PublisherTrueSoftware B.V.
LicenseMIT
Module formatESM only ("type": "module")
Public entryblendsdk/react → dist/index.js + dist/index.d.ts
React targetReact 19 function components and hooks
DistributionPrivate workspace package, consumed through the blendsdk umbrella
Workspace toolingNode.js >= 22, tsc, Vitest, Testing Library, jsdom

Key Features ​

  • BFF session authentication for OIDC — AuthProvider and useAuth() manage an HttpOnly cookie session held by a backend-for-frontend. The browser never handles access or refresh tokens. login(), logout(), and refresh() are exposed as actions, and the session is hydrated from the BFF's /me endpoint.
  • Automatic session renewal — with autoRefresh enabled (the default), the provider refreshes the session before expiresAt; refreshLeadTime controls how many seconds ahead of expiry the refresh starts. Manual refresh() returns a boolean result.
  • CSRF-aware client state — the per-session token returned by /me and /refresh is exposed as csrfToken, together with the configured csrfHeader name, so state-changing BFF calls can send it back.
  • Declarative authorization — AuthGuard gates an unauthenticated user to the login route, RequireAccess gates a signed-in user without the required grant to the not-authorized route, and Can conditionally renders individual UI. useAuthorization() exposes the same rules imperatively as roles, permissions, hasRole(), and can(), backed by blendsdk/authz.
  • Server-aligned, fail-closed checks — authorization is presentation only: the server remains the authority. Anonymous users and malformed roles/permissions claims produce an empty principal, so guards deny instead of throwing.
  • Asynchronous internationalization — I18nProvider accepts an application-supplied TranslationLoader, loads a default locale on mount, and exposes t() with interpolation and plurals through blendsdk/i18n. setLocale() re-fetches at runtime, reloadTranslations() refreshes the current locale, and onMissingTranslation reports unknown keys.
  • Global loading overlay — GlobalLoaderProvider and useGlobalLoader() control a full-screen, CSS-only spinner from anywhere in the tree. Spinner color, width, size, background, text color, z-index, and the text renderer are configurable; hiding the loader also clears its text.
  • Object-shaped local state — useObjectState() keeps one plain object per component, applies partial patches or functional updates, and resets by re-running the original factory. The setter and reset callbacks are stable across renders.
  • Type-complete public surface — every public value has exported companion types, including AuthConfig, AuthUser, AuthContextValue, ResolvedAuthConfig, UseAuthorizationResult, RequireAccessProps, CanProps, I18nProviderProps, TranslationLoader, GlobalLoaderConfig, and UseObjectStateResult. Hooks throw descriptive errors when used outside their provider.

When To Use ​

Use blendsdk/react when:

  • You are building a React 19 SPA against a BlendSDK BFF that exposes login, callback, logout, session, and refresh endpoints.
  • You want session-cookie authentication with no token storage, refresh scheduling, or OIDC handling in browser code.
  • UI visibility must follow server-issued roles and permissions while the server remains the enforcement point.
  • Translations are loaded asynchronously from an API, CDN, or bundler and locales switch without a page reload.
  • Long-running operations need one application-wide loading overlay instead of per-screen spinners.
  • A component owns a plain object of related fields — a form, filter panel, or editor — and you want partial updates without one useState per field.
  • You need optional React Router integration: only the redirecting guards require react-router; the providers and hooks do not.

Reach for something else when:

  • You need a styled component library or design system. This package supplies application infrastructure, not visuals.
  • Authentication is token-based in the browser or not fronted by a BFF. The auth module models a cookie session with /me and /refresh; endpoint paths are configurable, but the session contract is assumed.
  • You are on React 18 or earlier. The package targets React 19.

Architecture ​

The package is organized into four independent modules that share one public entry point and a common Provider/Context/Hook shape. Each module has its own barrel under src/, and only the root src/index.ts re-exports the public contract.

Module Map ​

ModulePublic surfaceRequiresResponsibility
Global loaderGlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoaderGlobalLoaderProvider around the hookFull-screen overlay with a CSS spinner, optional message, and configurable appearance
I18nI18nProvider, useTranslationsI18nProvider; expects GlobalLoaderProvider above itLoader-driven translations, t(), locale, setLocale(), reloadTranslations(), ready
AuthAuthProvider, AuthGuard, useAuth, useAuthorization, RequireAccess, Can, AUTH_DEFAULTSAuthProvider; the redirecting guards also need React RouterBFF/OIDC session state, actions, guards, role/permission predicates
StateuseObjectStatenonePartial-patch state for one plain object, with reset

Provider Composition ​

A typical application tree composes the providers from the outside in. Only the I18n-inside-GlobalLoader edge is required: I18nProvider uses the global loader while fetching translations. The auth subtree may sit inside or outside the i18n subtree depending on whether auth UI needs translations.

text
<GlobalLoaderProvider>                     overlay + useGlobalLoader()
└── <I18nProvider loader={...}>            translations + useTranslations()
    └── <AuthProvider config={{ basePath }}>
        ├── <AuthGuard> ... </AuthGuard>           authentication gate
        ├── <RequireAccess ...> ... </RequireAccess>   grant gate
        ├── <Can ...> ... </Can>                   element visibility
        └── application routes and components

useObjectState is provider-independent and can be used anywhere.

Authentication Model ​

Authentication follows the BFF pattern. login(returnTo?) navigates the browser to ${basePath}${endpoints.login}; the BFF performs the OIDC authorization-code flow and establishes an HttpOnly session cookie. AuthProvider then hydrates state from ${basePath}${endpoints.me}, which returns the user, the authorization decision, the session expiry, and the CSRF token. A POST to ${basePath}${endpoints.refresh} renews the session, automatically when autoRefresh is true and refreshLeadTime seconds before expiry. Logout goes through ${basePath}${endpoints.logout} and clears local state.

Two session flags are deliberately separate:

  • isAuthenticated means a user object is present.
  • authorized means the server returned a session that is not marked authorized: false. It is false before the first check, for anonymous or failed checks, for a session the application denied, and after logout. A signed-in but unauthorized session therefore has isAuthenticated === true and authorized === false.

All endpoint paths and behavioral defaults are merged from AUTH_DEFAULTS and the user-supplied AuthConfig into a fully resolved ResolvedAuthConfig on mount. The CSRF token is the only credential the client handles; the session cookie itself is not readable by JavaScript.

Design Patterns ​

  • Provider / Context / Hook — each feature owns state in a provider, carries it through a React context, and exposes a consumer hook that throws a descriptive error outside its provider.
  • Composition over configuration — capabilities are layered in JSX. I18nProvider composes the global loader; auth guards compose AuthProvider state.
  • Configuration resolution with defaults — AUTH_DEFAULTS is merged with AuthConfig into ResolvedAuthConfig; GlobalLoaderConfig has defaults for every property. Global loader config is captured on mount and is not reactive, so changing it requires remounting the provider.
  • Strategy / dependency injection — the application supplies the TranslationLoader, so translations can come from any source. Auth endpoint paths can be overridden relative to basePath.
  • Declarative guards — AuthGuard, RequireAccess, and Can express access rules in JSX; useAuthorization() is the imperative counterpart for logic that cannot be expressed as a wrapper.
  • Fail-closed authorization — non-array grants, non-string entries, and anonymous users all resolve to an empty principal, so requirements deny rather than crash.
  • Lazy factory and stable callbacks — useObjectState runs its factory lazily on mount, shallow-merges patches into the latest state, and keeps setState and reset stable across renders; reset stores a fresh object.
  • Single public entry point — internal modules are reachable only through the root barrel; the published contract is the set of symbols listed under src/index.ts.

Dependencies ​

DependencyVersionKindPurpose
react^19.0.0Peer, requiredContext, hooks, and component rendering
react-dom^19.0.0Peer, requiredDOM renderer for the host application
react-router^7.0.0Peer, optionalRedirects performed by AuthGuard and RequireAccess
blendsdk/authzWorkspaceRuntime dependencyAccessPrincipal, hasRole(), hasPermission()

The runtime footprint is React 19 plus the two internal BlendSDK libraries; the package does not bundle a UI framework or a state-management library. react-router is declared as an optional peer: install it only when the redirecting guard components are rendered.

Dependents. Consumers are BlendSDK React application packages. blendsdk/react is private in the monorepo and reaches end users only through the blendsdk umbrella package; it is not published standalone.

Installation in a host application. Install the umbrella and the peer packages together:

bash
npm install blendsdk react react-dom

Add react-router when using the guards:

bash
npm install blendsdk react react-dom react-router

Build. tsc emits ESM JavaScript and declarations into dist/. There is no CommonJS build and no CSS file to import; the loader injects its styles at runtime.

Minimum Example ​

The shortest complete example shows the two central pieces: a provider that owns session state and a hook that consumes it. AuthProvider hydrates from GET /api/auth/me and exposes login and logout actions; GlobalLoaderProvider supplies the application-wide overlay available to descendants.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, GlobalLoaderProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionBar() {
    const { user, isAuthenticated, isLoading, login, logout } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
        return <button onClick={() => login()}>Sign in</button>;
    }

    return <button onClick={() => void logout()}>Sign out ({user?.sub})</button>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
                <SessionBar />
            </AuthProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

SessionBar reads the session through useAuth(); isLoading covers the initial /me check, and login() redirects to the BFF login endpoint. The i18n and state modules compose in the same way — wrap with their provider where required, then consume with the matching hook. Their detailed contracts are covered in the module-specific documents.

react Core Concepts ​

blendsdk/react supplies application infrastructure, not visual components. Its public surface is organized around five concepts: a global loading overlay, asynchronous internationalization, a BFF-backed authentication session, declarative and imperative authorization, and object-shaped local state. Each concept follows the same shape: a provider owns state, a React context carries it, and a hook consumes it. With the exception of useObjectState, hooks throw a descriptive error when called outside their provider.

Two cross-cutting rules apply throughout. First, configuration is resolved with defaults: AuthProvider merges AuthConfig with AUTH_DEFAULTS, and GlobalLoaderProvider applies defaults to every omitted GlobalLoaderConfig property. Second, authorization is presentation only; the server remains the enforcement point.

ConceptPublic surfaceProvider requiredNotes
Global loaderGlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader, GlobalLoaderConfigGlobalLoaderProviderConfiguration captured on mount
InternationalizationI18nProvider, useTranslations, TranslationLoader, TranslateFunctionI18nProviderUses the global loader; mount inside it
AuthenticationAuthProvider, useAuth, AUTH_DEFAULTS, AuthConfig, AuthUser, AuthContextValue, ResolvedAuthConfigAuthProviderBFF/OIDC cookie session
AuthorizationuseAuthorization, AuthGuard, RequireAccess, Can, UseAuthorizationResultAuthProviderRedirecting gates need React Router
Object stateuseObjectState, ObjectStateSetter, ObjectStateReset, UseObjectStateResultNonePlain objects only

See the Overview for the package map and provider composition order.

Global Loader ​

What It Is ​

The global loader is one application-wide overlay with a CSS-drawn spinner and an optional message. GlobalLoaderProvider owns its visibility and text; useGlobalLoader() lets any descendant show or hide it and set the message. It is deliberately not a data-fetching or progress-tracking system: it renders a blocking visual state and nothing else. Typical uses are route transitions, session bootstrap, and save operations that should prevent interaction.

How It Works ​

  • The provider holds a single visible boolean and an optional text string. When visible, it renders a full-screen overlay above the application subtree. The spinner is rendered with CSS; there is no CSS file to import.
  • showLoader(true) displays the overlay. showLoader(false) hides it and clears the text. setText("...") changes the message but does not change visibility; pair it with showLoader(true). Passing null or "" clears the message.
  • By default the message renders in a paragraph element with the configured textColor, fontSize: 14px, and marginTop: 16px. textComponent replaces that renderer.
  • Configuration is captured on mount and is not reactive. Omitted properties use the defaults in the table below. To apply a different configuration, remount the provider.
  • The loader is a single visibility flag, not a reference-counted stack. Overlapping operations share the same overlay; a showLoader(false) from one operation hides it for all. Coordinate ownership or wrap a workflow in one component that sets and clears the loader.
  • useGlobalLoader() must be called inside GlobalLoaderProvider; outside, it throws an error that names the missing provider.

Complete Example ​

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function SaveButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText, visible } = useGlobalLoader();

    const save = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Saving changes…");
        showLoader(true);
        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/invoices/42", { method: "PUT" });
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Save failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not save invoice", error);
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void save()} disabled={visible}>
            {visible ? "Saving…" : "Save"}
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider
            config={{
                spinnerColor: "#25b09b",
                spinnerSize: 64,
                textColor: "#1f2933",
            }}
        >
            <SaveButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

Hook return value

NameType/SignatureDescription
showLoader(visible: boolean) => voidShows or hides the overlay. Passing false also clears the current text.
setText(text: string | null) => voidSets the message below the spinner. null or "" clears it.
visiblebooleanCurrent visibility of the overlay. Read-only.

Provider props and configuration

The Internationalization provider uses this overlay while fetching translations. Mount I18nProvider inside GlobalLoaderProvider when translations are loaded at runtime.

Internationalization ​

What It Is ​

I18nProvider loads translations asynchronously and exposes them through t(). The application supplies a TranslationLoader; the provider calls it for the initial locale, wraps the returned flat key/value map into a TranslationCatalog from blendsdk/i18n, and makes the catalog available to descendants. This keeps translation storage pluggable: an API, a CDN, or a bundler can all back the loader.

How It Works ​

  • On mount, the provider loads defaultLocale (default "en") by calling loader(locale). The loader returns Promise<Record<string, TranslationValue>>; the provider converts it into the catalog used by t().
  • t(key, params?) translates a key. params supplies interpolation values; a count parameter selects plural forms. Missing keys are reported through onMissingTranslation(key, locale) when that callback is provided.
  • setLocale(locale) switches the active locale and triggers a new loader call. reloadTranslations() re-fetches the current locale, for example after a server-side translation change. Translation fetches report progress through the global loader, so mount I18nProvider inside GlobalLoaderProvider.
  • ready is true after a successful load. The public context does not expose an error field; surface loader failures through your own logging or an error boundary.
  • defaultLocale is the mount-time default. Use setLocale() to change the active locale at runtime.
  • useTranslations() must be called inside I18nProvider; outside, it throws a descriptive error.

Complete Example ​

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Dashboard() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale, reloadTranslations, ready } = useTranslations();

    if (!ready) {
        return <p>Loading translations…</p>;
    }

    return (
        <section lang={locale}>
            <h1>{t("dashboard.title")}</h1>
            <p>{t("dashboard.welcome", { name: "Ada" })}</p>
            <p>{t("cart.items", { count: 3 })}</p>
            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setLocale(locale === "en" ? "nl" : "en")}
            >
                {t("language.switch")}
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={reloadTranslations}>
                {t("common.reload")}
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider
                loader={loadTranslations}
                defaultLocale="en"
                onMissingTranslation={(key, missingLocale) => {
                    console.warn(`Missing translation "${key}" for "${missingLocale}"`);
                }}
            >
                <Dashboard />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

Hook return value

NameType/SignatureDescription
t(key: string, params?: Record<string, unknown>) => stringTranslates a key with optional interpolation. A count parameter selects plural forms.
localestringActive locale.
setLocale(locale: string) => voidSwitches locale and re-fetches through the loader.
reloadTranslations() => voidRe-fetches translations for the current locale.
readybooleantrue when translations have loaded successfully.

Provider props and types

NameType/SignatureDescription

defaultLocalestring | undefinedLocale loaded on mount; default "en".
onMissingTranslation(key: string, locale: string) => void | undefinedCalled when a translation key is not found.

I18nProvider depends on the global loader for fetch feedback. Compose it inside GlobalLoaderProvider as shown in Global Loader. The TranslationLoader type is exported so application code can annotate its loader without importing the catalog internals.

Authentication Session ​

What It Is ​

AuthProvider manages an OIDC session established by a backend-for-frontend (BFF). The browser holds only an HttpOnly session cookie set by the BFF; it never stores access or refresh tokens. The provider hydrates the session from the BFF's me endpoint, exposes login/logout/refresh actions, schedules automatic renewal, and carries the per-session CSRF token. useAuth() is the consumer hook.

How It Works ​

  1. Configuration resolution. On mount, the provider merges the required basePath and optional AuthConfig values with AUTH_DEFAULTS. Endpoint paths are relative to basePath; the resolved object is available as useAuth().config with the ResolvedAuthConfig type.

  2. Session hydration. The provider checks the session with GET ${basePath}${endpoints.me}. isLoading is true during the initial check. A successful response supplies the user, the authorization decision, the expiry timestamp, and the CSRF token.

  3. Authentication versus authorization. isAuthenticated is derived from user !== null. authorized is the server's decision and is separate: it is true only when me returned a session that is not marked authorized: false. It is false before the first check, for anonymous or failed checks, for a session the application denied, and after logout. A signed-in but unauthorized session therefore has isAuthenticated === true and authorized === false.

  4. Actions. login(returnTo?) navigates the browser to the BFF login endpoint; the BFF performs the OIDC authorization-code flow and sets the session cookie. It is a navigation, not an async API. logout() calls the BFF logout endpoint and clears local state. refresh() calls the BFF refresh endpoint and resolves to true on success and false on failure.

  5. Automatic renewal. With autoRefresh enabled (the default), the provider schedules a refresh refreshLeadTime seconds before expiresAt (default 60). Manual refresh() remains available.

  6. CSRF. The token returned by me or refresh is exposed as csrfToken; send it in the header named by config.csrfHeader (default x-csrf-token) on state-changing BFF calls. csrfToken is a snapshot: depending on server configuration, the token can be regenerated when session-id rotation is enabled. A token replaced by another browsing context is not observed here until the next session check, so a request made with the outdated token can be rejected with 403.

  7. Hook contract. useAuth() must be called inside AuthProvider; outside, it throws a descriptive error.

Complete Example ​

tsx
import { AUTH_DEFAULTS, AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    endpoints: {
        ...AUTH_DEFAULTS.endpoints,
        me: "/session",
    },
    loginPath: "/sign-in",
    defaultReturnTo: "/dashboard",
    autoRefresh: true,
    refreshLeadTime: 30,
};

function SessionPanel() {
    const {
        user,
        isAuthenticated,
        isLoading,
        authorized,
        expiresAt,
        csrfToken,
        config,
        login,
        logout,
        refresh,
    } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated || user === null) {
        return (
            <button type="button" onClick={() => login("/invoices")}>
                Sign in
            </button>
        );
    }

    const handleRefresh = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            const refreshed = await refresh();
            if (!refreshed) {
                console.warn("Session refresh failed");
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not refresh session", error);
        }
    };

    const handleDelete = async (): Promise<void> => {
        const headers: Record<string, string> = {};
        if (csrfToken !== null) {
            headers[config.csrfHeader] = csrfToken;
        }

        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/bff/invoices/42", {
                method: "DELETE",
                headers,
            });
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Delete failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not delete invoice", error);
        }
    };

    const handleLogout = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            await logout();
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not sign out", error);
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Signed in as {user.sub}</p>
            <p>Authorized: {authorized ? "yes" : "no"}</p>
            <p>
                Expires:{" "}
                {expiresAt === null
                    ? "unknown"
                    : new Date(expiresAt * 1000).toLocaleString()}
            </p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleRefresh()}>
                Refresh session
            </button>
            {authorized ? (
                <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleDelete()}>
                    Delete invoice
                </button>
            ) : (
                <p>The server has not authorized this session for invoice changes.</p>
            )}
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleLogout()}>
                Sign out
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <SessionPanel />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

useAuth() return value

NameType/SignatureDescription
userAuthUser | nullCurrent user; null when anonymous.
isAuthenticatedbooleantrue when user !== null.
isLoadingbooleantrue during the initial session check.
login(returnTo?: string) => voidNavigates to the BFF login endpoint, optionally with a return path.
logout() => Promise<void>Calls the BFF logout endpoint and clears local state.

AuthConfig properties and defaults

NameType/SignatureDescription

AuthUser shape

NameType/SignatureDescription
substringRequired OIDC subject identifier.
[key: string]unknownAdditional identity-provider claims, including roles and permissions.

isAuthenticated and authorized answer different questions. A session can be authenticated but not authorized. authorized is false before the first me check, for anonymous or failed checks, for a session the application denied, and after logout.

endpoints.login is the BFF endpoint used by login(); loginPath is the frontend route used by AuthGuard. They are different paths and can have different values.

Route-level authentication is provided by AuthGuard; see Authorization Predicates and Gates.

Authorization Predicates and Gates ​

What It Is ​

Authorization answers two questions about the current session: does the user hold a role, and does the user hold a permission? useAuthorization() exposes the roles, permissions, and the hasRole() / can() predicates. AuthGuard, RequireAccess, and Can apply the same checks declaratively. The layer is intentionally presentation-only: the server is the authority, and client-side checks only decide what to render.

How It Works ​

  • useAuthorization() reads the user from useAuth(), so it must be used inside AuthProvider.
  • Grants come from the session user's roles and permissions properties. These are the canonical grants the server stored on the session user after translating the provider identity. The hook treats the claims as untrusted runtime data: a non-array value becomes an empty list, non-string entries are ignored, and duplicates are removed with the first occurrence winning. An anonymous user or a malformed grants object produces an empty principal, so requirements fail closed instead of throwing.
  • The result is memoized on the user. roles and permissions are readonly arrays, and hasRole/can are stable while the user object is unchanged. Evaluation delegates to hasRole() and hasPermission() from blendsdk/authz.
  • Declarative gates: AuthGuard gates authentication and redirects unauthenticated users to config.loginPath; RequireAccess gates a required grant and redirects signed-in users without it to config.notAuthorizedPath; Can conditionally renders a UI fragment without redirecting. AuthGuard and RequireAccess perform redirects and therefore need the optional react-router peer. Can and the hook do not.
  • Server authority: a hidden button is a convenience, never a security boundary. The BFF must enforce the same grants on every state-changing and data-reading endpoint.

Complete Example ​

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuthorization } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceToolbar() {
    const { roles, permissions, hasRole, can } = useAuthorization();

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Roles: {roles.length > 0 ? roles.join(", ") : "none"}</p>
            <p>
                Permissions:{" "}
                {permissions.length > 0 ? permissions.join(", ") : "none"}
            </p>
            {hasRole("finance") && <strong>Finance</strong>}
            {can("invoice:write") && <button type="button">Edit invoice</button>}
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoiceToolbar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

useAuthorization() return value

NameType/SignatureDescription
rolesreadonly string[]Roles held by the current user.
permissionsreadonly string[]Permissions held by the current user.
hasRole(role: string) => booleanReports whether the user holds a role.
can(permission: string) => booleanReports whether the user holds a permission.

Principal derivation

SourceRule
user.rolesMust be an array. Non-array values become an empty list; non-string entries are ignored; duplicates are removed with the first occurrence winning.
user.permissionsSame rules as user.roles.
Anonymous userEmpty principal; every check returns false.
Malformed grantsEmpty principal; checks fail closed instead of throwing.

Declarative gates

ComponentBehaviorRouter required
AuthGuardGates authentication; redirects unauthenticated users to config.loginPath.Yes
RequireAccessGates a required grant; redirects signed-in users without it to config.notAuthorizedPath.Yes
CanConditionally renders children when the required grant is held.No

A user can be authenticated and still unauthorized: isAuthenticated is about having a session, while authorized is the server's decision. useAuthorization() reads the grants on that session; it does not change the server's decision.

Object-Shaped Local State ​

What It Is ​

useObjectState manages one plain object as local component state. It is aimed at clusters of related fields — forms, filter panels, editors — where separate useState calls would be noisy. The hook returns the object, a patch-oriented setter, and a reset function. It is provider-independent and does not participate in authentication, internationalization, or the global loader.

How It Works ​

  • const [state, setState, reset] = useObjectState<T>(() => initial). The factory runs lazily on mount. reset calls the original factory again and stores a fresh object, so the reset baseline is not the initial object reference.
  • setState accepts either a partial patch or (previous) => patch. It applies the patch with a shallow spread inside React's functional updater: { ...previous, ...patch }. Consecutive updates in the same event therefore build on the latest state, not on a stale render value.
  • The setter and reset callbacks have stable identities across renders. Code that previously listed setState in a dependency array and read state without listing it should add the state values it reads, or use the functional updater form.
  • The contract is plain objects. Arrays, class instances, and function values are outside the contract because object spreading drops prototypes and array behavior. Nested objects are replaced, not deep-merged. Setting a property to undefined leaves the key present.
  • T can be an interface; the hook does not require an index signature, and Partial<T> patches are checked against the declared shape.
  • The factory must be pure and return a new plain object on every call. React StrictMode may invoke it twice in development, and reset invokes it again. reset uses the factory from the first render; changing the create argument later does not change the reset baseline.

Complete Example ​

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface FilterState {
    query: string;
    status: "all" | "open" | "closed";
    page: number;
}

function isStatus(value: string): value is FilterState["status"] {
    return value === "all" || value === "open" || value === "closed";
}

export function InvoiceFilters() {
    const [filters, setFilters, resetFilters] = useObjectState<FilterState>(() => ({
        query: "",
        status: "all",
        page: 1,
    }));

    const nextPage = (): void => {
        setFilters((previous) => ({ page: previous.page + 1 }));
    };

    return (
        <form>
            <label>
                Query
                <input
                    value={filters.query}
                    onChange={(event) =>
                        setFilters({ query: event.target.value, page: 1 })
                    }
                />
            </label>
            <label>
                Status
                <select
                    value={filters.status}
                    onChange={(event) => {
                        const value = event.target.value;
                        if (isStatus(value)) {
                            setFilters({ status: value, page: 1 });
                        }
                    }}
                >
                    <option value="all">All</option>
                    <option value="open">Open</option>
                    <option value="closed">Closed</option>
                </select>
            </label>
            <button type="button" onClick={nextPage}>
                Next page ({filters.page})
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={resetFilters}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

Key Methods and Properties ​

Parameters and return value

NameType/SignatureDescription
create() => TLazy factory for the initial object. Must return a new plain object on every call.
stateTCurrent object.
setState(update: Partial<T> | ((previous: T) => Partial<T>)) => voidShallow-merges a patch into the latest state.
reset() => voidRe-runs the original factory and stores a fresh object.
UseObjectStateResult<T>[T, ObjectStateSetter<T>, ObjectStateReset]Tuple returned by the hook.

Contract

ContractBehavior
State shapePlain objects only. Arrays, class instances, and function values are unsupported.
Merge depthShallow. Nested objects are replaced, not deep-merged.
undefined valuesSetting a property to undefined leaves the key present.
FactoryMust be pure and return a new plain object each call. React StrictMode may invoke it twice in development.
Callback identitysetState and reset are stable across renders.
Reset baselineThe factory captured on the first render; a later create argument does not replace it.

useObjectState does not delete keys. To represent an absent value, make the property optional in T and set it to undefined; the key remains present with the value undefined.

Compatibility note: the setter and reset are stable across renders. If existing code listed setState in a dependency array and read state without listing it, add the state values it reads or use the functional updater form. Relying on a changing setter identity is not supported.

react Basic Usage ​

blendsdk/react provides the React application layer for BlendSDK: BFF-backed authentication, authorization predicates, asynchronous internationalization, a global loading overlay, and object-shaped local state. This guide starts with installation, then introduces each module through progressively larger examples.

Installation ​

blendsdk/react is a private workspace package consumed through the blendsdk umbrella. Install the umbrella plus the required React 19 peers; keep importing from blendsdk/react in source files.

Package managerCommand
npmnpm install blendsdk react react-dom
yarnyarn add blendsdk react react-dom
pnpmpnpm add blendsdk react react-dom

react and react-dom are required peers. The redirecting guards (AuthGuard and RequireAccess) also need the optional react-router peer:

bash
npm install blendsdk react react-dom react-router

For yarn or pnpm, use the same package list with yarn add or pnpm add.

Quick Start ​

The smallest self-contained setup uses the global loader. Wrap a subtree with GlobalLoaderProvider, then consume the loader from a descendant with useGlobalLoader().

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function LoaderButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();
    const run = (): void => {
        setText("Loading…");
        showLoader(true);
        window.setTimeout(() => showLoader(false), 1200);
    };

    return <button type="button" onClick={run}>Load for 1.2 seconds</button>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <LoaderButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Clicking the button displays the full-screen overlay for 1.2 seconds. showLoader(false) hides it and clears the message.

Fundamentals ​

Provider-backed features follow the same pattern: a provider owns state, a React context carries it, and a hook exposes it. The usual composition order is GlobalLoaderProvider outermost, I18nProvider inside it, and AuthProvider wherever session state is needed. Each subsection below introduces one module.

Global Loader ​

The global loader is one application-wide overlay with a CSS spinner and optional text. Start with showLoader(true) and showLoader(false); setText adds context while visible.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function SaveButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText, visible } = useGlobalLoader();

    const save = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Saving invoice…");
        showLoader(true);
        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/invoices/42", { method: "PUT" });
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Save failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not save invoice", error);
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" disabled={visible} onClick={() => void save()}>
            Save invoice
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider
            config={{
                spinnerColor: "#25b09b",
                spinnerSize: 64,
                textColor: "#1f2933",
            }}
        >
            <SaveButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}
  • showLoader(false) hides the overlay and clears the current text. setText(null) or setText("") clears only the text.
  • The loader is a single visibility flag, not a reference-counted stack. Overlapping operations share the same overlay; one showLoader(false) hides it for all.
  • Configuration is captured on mount. Remount the provider to apply a different GlobalLoaderConfig.
  • useGlobalLoader() must be called inside GlobalLoaderProvider; outside, it throws a descriptive error.

Internationalization ​

I18nProvider loads translations asynchronously through an application-supplied TranslationLoader. The provider calls the loader for the default locale on mount, then exposes t(), locale, setLocale(), reloadTranslations(), and ready.

tsx
import {
    GlobalLoaderProvider,
    I18nProvider,
    useTranslations,
} from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Greeting() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale, ready } = useTranslations();

    if (!ready) {
        return <p>Loading translations…</p>;
    }

    return (
        <section lang={locale}>
            <h1>{t("greeting.title")}</h1>
            <p>{t("greeting.body", { name: "Ada" })}</p>
            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setLocale(locale === "en" ? "nl" : "en")}
            >
                {t("language.switch")}
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <Greeting />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}
  • t(key, params?) supports interpolation; a count parameter selects plural forms.
  • setLocale() switches the active locale and triggers a new loader call. reloadTranslations() re-fetches the current locale.
  • ready is false until translations load successfully.
  • Mount I18nProvider inside GlobalLoaderProvider: translation fetches report progress through the global loader.
  • onMissingTranslation(key, locale) reports unknown keys when provided.
  • useTranslations() must be called inside I18nProvider; outside, it throws a descriptive error.

Authentication ​

AuthProvider manages an OIDC session established by a backend-for-frontend. The browser holds only the BFF's HttpOnly session cookie; access and refresh tokens never reach browser code. The provider hydrates the session from the me endpoint and exposes actions through useAuth().

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionPanel() {
    const { user, isAuthenticated, isLoading, login, logout } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
        return (
            <button type="button" onClick={() => login("/invoices")}>
                Sign in
            </button>
        );
    }

    const handleLogout = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            await logout();
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not sign out", error);
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Signed in as {user?.sub}</p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleLogout()}>
                Sign out
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SessionPanel />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}
  • isLoading is true during the initial me check. isAuthenticated is derived from user !== null.
  • login(returnTo?) navigates the browser to the BFF login endpoint. It is a navigation, not an async function.
  • logout() calls the BFF logout endpoint and clears local state.
  • isAuthenticated and authorized answer different questions: a signed-in session can still be unauthorized by the server.
  • refresh() renews the session and resolves to true on success. With autoRefresh enabled, renewal is scheduled before expiresAt.
  • csrfToken and config.csrfHeader support state-changing BFF calls; send the token in the configured header.
  • useAuth() must be called inside AuthProvider; outside, it throws a descriptive error.

Authorization ​

Authorization reads the canonical grants stored on the session user. useAuthorization() exposes roles, permissions, hasRole(), and can(); it must be used inside AuthProvider.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuthorization } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceToolbar() {
    const { roles, permissions, hasRole, can } = useAuthorization();

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Roles: {roles.length > 0 ? roles.join(", ") : "none"}</p>
            <p>
                Permissions:{" "}
                {permissions.length > 0 ? permissions.join(", ") : "none"}
            </p>
            {hasRole("finance") && <strong>Finance</strong>}
            {can("invoice:write") && <button type="button">Edit invoice</button>}
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoiceToolbar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}
  • Grants are read from the session user's roles and permissions properties. Malformed values, non-string entries, and anonymous users produce an empty principal, so checks fail closed instead of throwing.
  • The result is memoized on the user; hasRole and can stay stable while the user object is unchanged.
  • Authorization is presentation only. A hidden button is a convenience, never a security boundary; the server must enforce the same grants.
  • The package also exports Can for conditional rendering and AuthGuard / RequireAccess for route-level redirects. The redirecting guards require the optional react-router peer.

Object State ​

useObjectState manages one plain object as local component state. It returns the current object, a patch-oriented setter, and a reset function. No provider is required.

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface ProfileState {
    name: string;
    age: number;
}

export function ProfileForm() {
    const [profile, setProfile, resetProfile] = useObjectState<ProfileState>(() => ({
        name: "",
        age: 0,
    }));

    return (
        <div>
            <label>
                Name{" "}
                <input
                    value={profile.name}
                    onChange={(event) => setProfile({ name: event.target.value })}
                />
            </label>
            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setProfile((previous) => ({ age: previous.age + 1 }))}
            >
                Age: {profile.age}
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={resetProfile}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}
  • The factory runs lazily on mount. reset calls the original factory again and stores a fresh object.
  • setProfile({ name: "..." }) shallow-merges a partial patch into the latest state.
  • The functional form, setProfile((previous) => ({ age: previous.age + 1 })), builds on the latest state even when several updates happen in one event.
  • The contract is plain objects. Arrays, class instances, and function values are unsupported; nested objects are replaced, not deep-merged.
  • setProfile and resetProfile keep the same identity across renders.

Configuration ​

Providers merge omitted values with defaults. AUTH_DEFAULTS is exported for reading the auth defaults; the global loader captures its configuration on mount, and the i18n provider uses defaultLocale as its mount-time locale.

A common auth override uses AUTH_DEFAULTS to keep the default endpoints while replacing one path:

tsx
import { AUTH_DEFAULTS, AuthProvider } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { ReactNode } from "react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    endpoints: {
        ...AUTH_DEFAULTS.endpoints,
        me: "/session",
    },
    loginPath: "/sign-in",
    defaultReturnTo: "/dashboard",
    refreshLeadTime: 30,
};

export function AuthRoot({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
    return <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>{children}</AuthProvider>;
}

Auth Configuration ​

NameTypeDefaultDescription
basePathstringRequiredBase path for all BFF auth endpoints, such as /api/auth.
endpoints{ login?: string; callback?: string; logout?: string; me?: string; refresh?: string }{ login: "/login", callback: "/callback", logout: "/logout", me: "/me", refresh: "/refresh" }Endpoint paths relative to basePath.
loginPathstring"/login"Frontend route used by AuthGuard for sign-in.
notAuthorizedPathstring"/not-authorized"Frontend route used by RequireAccess when a grant is missing.
defaultReturnTostring"/"Frontend path to redirect to after login.
autoRefreshbooleantrueRefresh the session before expiry.
refreshLeadTimenumber60Seconds before expiry to trigger the refresh.
csrfHeaderstring"x-csrf-token"Header carrying the per-session CSRF token.

endpoints.login is the BFF endpoint used by login(); loginPath is the frontend route used by AuthGuard. They are different paths. Resolved auth configuration is available as useAuth().config with the ResolvedAuthConfig type.

Global Loader Configuration ​

NameTypeDefaultDescription
spinnerColorstring"#888888"CSS color of the spinner arc.
spinnerWidthnumber3Spinner arc width (padding), in pixels.
backgroundColorstring"#fafafa"Full-screen overlay background color.
spinnerSizenumber50Spinner diameter, in pixels.
textColorstring"#888888"CSS color of the text below the spinner.
zIndexnumber999999Stacking order of the overlay.
textComponent(props: { text: string; textColor: string }) => ReactElementParagraph rendererCustom renderer for the message below the spinner.

Global loader configuration is captured on mount and is not reactive. Remount GlobalLoaderProvider to apply different values.

I18n Configuration ​

NameTypeDefaultDescription
loaderTranslationLoaderRequiredAsync source for translations; receives the locale and returns a flat key/value map.
defaultLocalestring"en"Locale loaded on mount. Use setLocale() to change it at runtime.
onMissingTranslation(key: string, locale: string) => voidundefinedCalled when a translation key is not found.

Object State Input ​

There is no provider-level configuration for useObjectState; its only input is the factory.

NameTypeDefaultDescription
create() => TRequiredLazy factory for the initial plain object. Must return a new object on every call.

Error Handling ​

blendsdk/react does not export custom error classes. Failures fall into three categories.

CategoryError formMeaningHandling
Provider misuseError thrown during renderA hook was called outside its required provider.Fix the provider composition; treat this as a configuration error.
Auth action failureRejected promise from logout(); refresh() can also failA BFF request did not complete as expected.Use try/catch; check the boolean result from refresh().
Translation load failureRejected TranslationLoader promiseThe translation source was unreachable or returned an invalid response.Handle inside the loader and return a fallback, or report through application-level error handling.

Provider Misuse ​

These errors are thrown by hooks during render when the required provider is missing:

HookRequired providerError message
useGlobalLoaderGlobalLoaderProvideruseGlobalLoader() must be used within a <GlobalLoaderProvider>. Wrap your component tree with <GlobalLoaderProvider> to use this hook.
useTranslationsI18nProvideruseTranslations() must be used within an <I18nProvider>. Wrap your component tree with <I18nProvider> to use this hook.
useAuthAuthProvideruseAuth() must be used within an <AuthProvider>. Wrap your component tree with <AuthProvider> to use this hook.
useAuthorizationAuthProvider (through useAuth)Throws the useAuth() message when no AuthProvider is present.

These are developer errors, not recoverable runtime states. Correct the provider tree rather than catching them in component logic.

Async Auth Actions ​

logout() returns a promise; refresh() resolves to true on success and reports an unsuccessful renewal as false. Keep the UI deterministic by handling both outcomes.

tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionActions() {
    const { logout, refresh } = useAuth();
    const [errorMessage, setErrorMessage] = useState<string | null>(null);

    const handleRefresh = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setErrorMessage(null);
        try {
            const refreshed = await refresh();
            if (!refreshed) {
                setErrorMessage("The session could not be refreshed.");
            }
        } catch (error) {
            setErrorMessage(
                error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unexpected refresh failure.",
            );
        }
    };

    const handleLogout = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setErrorMessage(null);
        try {
            await logout();
        } catch (error) {
            setErrorMessage(
                error instanceof Error ? error.message : "Unexpected logout failure.",
            );
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            {errorMessage !== null && <p role="alert">{errorMessage}</p>}
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleRefresh()}>
                Refresh session
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleLogout()}>
                Sign out
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SessionActions />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Translation Loader Failures ​

I18nContextValue exposes ready but no error field. Decide in the loader whether a failure should propagate to an application error boundary or fall back to an empty catalog.

typescript
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    try {
        const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
        if (!response.ok) {
            throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
        }
        return response.json();
    } catch (error) {
        console.error(`Could not load translations for ${locale}`, error);
        return {};
    }
};

The example logs the failure and returns an empty catalog. With onMissingTranslation, unresolved keys can still be reported while the application remains renderable.

react Advanced Patterns ​

This document collects patterns that combine more than one capability of blendsdk/react: the provider tree, the asynchronous BFF session, CSRF-aware requests, grant-driven UI, global-loader ownership, object-shaped form state, and expiry handling. Every example is self-contained — it imports only from blendsdk/react and React — so it can be pasted into an application module and compiled without additional context. Patterns cross-reference each other where composition helps, but each one stands alone.

#PatternCombines
1Compose the provider tree onceGlobal loader, I18n, auth
2Gate content on an asynchronous sessionAuth state, AuthGuard, RequireAccess
3Write CSRF-aware BFF requestsAuth session, fetch
4Drive UI from grantsuseAuthorization, Can
5Scope loader ownershipGlobal loader
6Save object-shaped forms through the BFFObject state, auth, I18n, loader
7Renew an expiring sessionAuth state, I18n

1. Compose the Provider Tree Once ​

When to use it. Always. Every BlendSDK React application mounts GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, and AuthProvider exactly once, at the root of the tree. Put that composition in a dedicated module so the required order is fixed, configuration is typed in one place, and feature code only ever imports hooks.

tsx
import {
    AuthProvider,
    GlobalLoaderProvider,
    I18nProvider,
    useAuth,
    useTranslations,
    type AuthConfig,
    type TranslationLoader,
} from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    loginPath: "/login",
    notAuthorizedPath: "/not-authorized",
    defaultReturnTo: "/dashboard",
    autoRefresh: true,
    refreshLeadTime: 120,
};

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Dashboard() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale, ready } = useTranslations();
    const { user, isAuthenticated, isLoading, login } = useAuth();

    if (!ready) {
        // Translations are not loaded yet: render boot text without t().
        return <p role="status">Preparing application…</p>;
    }

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p role="status">{t("session.checking")}</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated || user === null) {
        return (
            <button type="button" onClick={() => login()}>
                {t("auth.signIn")}
            </button>
        );
    }

    return (
        <section lang={locale}>
            <h1>{t("dashboard.title")}</h1>
            <p>{t("dashboard.welcome", { name: user.sub })}</p>
            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setLocale(locale === "en" ? "nl" : "en")}
            >
                {t("language.switch")}
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider config={{ spinnerColor: "#25b09b", spinnerSize: 56 }}>
            <I18nProvider
                loader={loadTranslations}
                defaultLocale="en"
                onMissingTranslation={(key, missingLocale) => {
                    console.warn(`[i18n] missing "${key}" for "${missingLocale}"`);
                }}
            >
                <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
                    <Dashboard />
                </AuthProvider>
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. The three providers have a real dependency order. I18nProvider reports translation fetches through the global loader, so it must sit inside GlobalLoaderProvider. The auth subtree sits inside I18nProvider so sign-in buttons, denied pages, and session banners can be translated. Encoding that order in one component makes the constraint impossible to violate accidentally, keeps AuthConfig type-checked in one place, and lets every feature module depend on hooks only — which is also what makes those modules testable without wiring the whole application.

Caveats and performance.

  • GlobalLoaderProvider captures its config on mount and is not reactive. To change spinner colors or size, remount the provider — do not pass a new object and expect a change.
  • Keep authConfig as a module-level constant rather than an inline object literal. Endpoint resolution, refresh scheduling, and session hydration happen on mount; a stable configuration reference documents that intent and avoids accidental provider remounts when the tree re-renders.
  • Do not call t() before ready is true. The catalog is empty until the loader resolves; render provider-independent boot text instead of translation keys.
  • Never mount these providers per route. Remounting AuthProvider re-runs the /me session check and resets auth state.
  • Every context update re-renders every consumer of that context. Keeping the provider at the root is correct, but keep heavy, non-auth subtrees out of components that only consume useAuth() for a single boolean.

2. Gate Content on an Asynchronous Session ​

When to use it. Every authenticated area of the application — dashboards, settings, admin screens. The session check is asynchronous (isLoading covers the initial /me call), and the answer is two-dimensional: the user may be signed in but not authorized by the server.

Before, each page repeats the rule and gets it subtly wrong:

tsx
function InvoicesPage() {
    const { isAuthenticated, login } = useAuth();

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
        login();      // side effect during render
        return null;  // also renders while isLoading is still true
    }

    return <main>Invoices</main>;
}

After, the bootstrap gate renders the loading state once, AuthGuard owns the redirect, and RequireAccess owns the grant check:

tsx
import type { ReactNode } from "react";
import {
    AuthGuard,
    AuthProvider,
    Can,
    RequireAccess,
    useAuth,
    type AuthConfig,
} from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    loginPath: "/login",
    notAuthorizedPath: "/not-authorized",
    defaultReturnTo: "/invoices",
};

function SessionBootstrap({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
    const { isLoading } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p role="status">Checking your session…</p>;
    }

    return <>{children}</>;
}

function InvoicesPage() {
    const { user, authorized } = useAuth();

    return (
        <main>
            <h1>Invoices</h1>
            <p>
                Signed in as {user?.sub ?? "unknown"} —{" "}
                {authorized ? "authorized by the server" : "not authorized by the server"}
            </p>

            <Can permission="invoice:write">
                <button type="button">New invoice</button>
            </Can>

            <Can permission="invoice:export">
                <button type="button">Export</button>
            </Can>
        </main>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <SessionBootstrap>
                <AuthGuard>
                    <RequireAccess permission="invoices:read">
                        <InvoicesPage />
                    </RequireAccess>
                </AuthGuard>
            </SessionBootstrap>
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. The three failure modes of hand-rolled gates disappear at once: no side effect during render, no flash of unauthenticated content while isLoading is true, and no page-level duplication of the redirect policy. The redirect destinations come from the resolved configuration (loginPath, notAuthorizedPath, defaultReturnTo), so changing where the app sends anonymous users is a one-line configuration change instead of a search across pages. Can then handles the in-page, non-redirecting case without repeating hooks.

Caveats and performance.

  • AuthGuard and RequireAccess navigate, so they require the optional react-router peer. Can and useAuth() do not.
  • The bootstrap gate is a user-experience concern, not a security control. The BFF must reject unauthorized requests regardless of what the client renders.
  • isAuthenticated and authorized are different questions. A session can be signed in and denied by the server. Surface that state explicitly rather than treating it as “logged out”:
tsx
function SessionDeniedNotice() {
    const { isAuthenticated, authorized } = useAuth();

    if (!isAuthenticated || authorized) {
        return null;
    }

    return <p role="alert">Signed in, but the server has not authorized this session.</p>;
}
  • Keep SessionBootstrap above the guards, not inside each page: it renders once per navigation instead of once per route component instance.
  • Can is presentation only. Hiding a button never protects an endpoint; the server enforces the same grant.

3. Write CSRF-Aware BFF Requests ​

When to use it. Any state-changing call to the BFF (POST, PUT, PATCH, DELETE). Those requests must carry the per-session CSRF token in the header named by config.csrfHeader, and the token is only available through useAuth(). Wrapping that in one hook removes the per-call header bookkeeping and gives every failure a single shape.

tsx
import { useCallback, useEffect, useState } from "react";
import { AuthProvider, useAuth, type AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = { basePath: "/api/auth" };

type HttpMethod = "GET" | "POST" | "PUT" | "PATCH" | "DELETE";

interface BffRequestOptions {
    method?: HttpMethod;
    body?: unknown;
    signal?: AbortSignal;
}

class BffError extends Error {
    readonly status: number;

    constructor(message: string, status: number) {
        super(message);
        this.name = "BffError";
        this.status = status;
    }
}

function useBffRequest() {
    const { csrfToken, config } = useAuth();

    return useCallback(
        async <TResponse,>(
            path: string,
            options: BffRequestOptions = {},
        ): Promise<TResponse | null> => {
            const method = options.method ?? "GET";
            const headers: Record<string, string> = { accept: "application/json" };

            if (options.body !== undefined) {
                headers["content-type"] = "application/json";
            }

            if (method !== "GET" && csrfToken !== null) {
                headers[config.csrfHeader] = csrfToken;
            }

            const response = await fetch(path, {
                method,
                headers,
                body: options.body === undefined ? undefined : JSON.stringify(options.body),
                credentials: "same-origin",
                signal: options.signal,
            });

            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new BffError(
                    `${method} ${path} failed with ${response.status}`,
                    response.status,
                );
            }

            if (response.status === 204) {
                return null;
            }

            const payload: TResponse = await response.json();
            return payload;
        },
        [csrfToken, config.csrfHeader],
    );
}

interface InvoiceSummary {
    id: string;
    total: number;
}

function InvoiceList() {
    const request = useBffRequest();
    const [invoices, setInvoices] = useState<InvoiceSummary[]>([]);
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        const controller = new AbortController();

        const load = async (): Promise<void> => {
            try {
                const data = await request<InvoiceSummary[]>("/api/bff/invoices", {
                    signal: controller.signal,
                });
                setInvoices(data ?? []);
            } catch (caught) {
                if (controller.signal.aborted) {
                    return;
                }
                setError(caught instanceof BffError ? caught.message : "Could not load invoices");
            }
        };

        void load();
        return () => controller.abort();
    }, [request]);

    const remove = async (id: string): Promise<void> => {
        setError(null);
        try {
            await request<null>(`/api/bff/invoices/${id}`, { method: "DELETE" });
            setInvoices((previous) => previous.filter((invoice) => invoice.id !== id));
        } catch (caught) {
            setError(caught instanceof BffError ? caught.message : "Could not delete invoice");
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            {error !== null && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
            <ul>
                {invoices.map((invoice) => (
                    <li key={invoice.id}>
                        {invoice.id} — {invoice.total.toFixed(2)}
                        <button type="button" onClick={() => void remove(invoice.id)}>
                            Delete
                        </button>
                    </li>
                ))}
            </ul>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <InvoiceList />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. The CSRF header is easy to forget on exactly the calls that need it, and the consequences are intermittent 403 responses that are hard to reproduce. Centralizing the header name, the token lookup, JSON encoding, abort support, and the error shape means every mutation behaves the same way and every caller can discriminate on status. Typed payloads (request<InvoiceSummary[]>) keep response handling honest without scattering casts through components. 204 No Content is modelled explicitly as null, so callers do not have to guess.

Caveats and performance.

  • The returned function is recreated when csrfToken changes — after the initial /me resolves and after every refresh. Effects that list request in their dependency array re-run; in the example that refetches the list, which is usually the behaviour you want after a session renewal. If you need a stable identity, hold the token in a ref updated in an effect, at the cost of occasionally sending the previous token.
  • csrfToken is a snapshot. When session-id rotation is enabled, a token replaced by another browsing context is not observed until the next session check, so a request made with an outdated token can be rejected with 403. Treat BffError.status === 403 as retryable after a refresh() and a re-render — never retry blindly in a loop.
  • credentials: "same-origin" assumes the SPA and the BFF share an origin, which is the point of the BFF pattern. A cross-origin split requires CORS credentials handling and changes the CSRF story; do not adopt it casually.
  • BffError does not parse structured error bodies. If your BFF returns problem details, extend the class with a parsed payload rather than parsing ad hoc at call sites.
  • Combine this with the loader scope from pattern 5 rather than toggling showLoader inside individual call sites.

4. Drive UI from Grants ​

When to use it. Toolbars, navigation, and action lists whose entries depend on roles or permissions. The naive version scatters string comparisons through JSX and re-evaluates them in inconsistent ways:

tsx
const { permissions } = useAuthorization();
const canEdit = permissions.includes("invoice:write");
const canDelete = permissions.includes("invoice:delete") || permissions.includes("invoice:admin");

The table-driven version keeps each permission next to its label and filters once:

tsx
import { useMemo, useState } from "react";
import {
    AuthProvider,
    Can,
    useAuthorization,
    type AuthConfig,
} from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = { basePath: "/api/auth" };

interface ToolbarAction {
    id: string;
    label: string;
    permission: string;
}

interface InvoiceToolbarProps {
    invoiceId: string;
    onAction: (actionId: string) => void;
}

function InvoiceToolbar({ invoiceId, onAction }: InvoiceToolbarProps) {
    const { can, hasRole, roles, permissions } = useAuthorization();

    const actions = useMemo<readonly ToolbarAction[]>(() => {
        const candidates: ToolbarAction[] = [
            { id: "edit", label: "Edit", permission: "invoice:write" },
            { id: "approve", label: "Approve", permission: "invoice:approve" },
            { id: "delete", label: "Delete", permission: "invoice:delete" },
        ];
        return candidates.filter((action) => can(action.permission));
    }, [can]);

    return (
        <section>
            <h2>Invoice {invoiceId}</h2>
            <p>
                Roles: {roles.length > 0 ? roles.join(", ") : "none"} · Permissions held:{" "}
                {permissions.length}
            </p>

            {hasRole("finance") && <p>Finance view available</p>}

            {actions.length === 0 ? (
                <p>No actions are available for this invoice.</p>
            ) : (
                <div>
                    {actions.map((action) => (
                        <button
                            key={action.id}
                            type="button"
                            onClick={() => onAction(action.id)}
                        >
                            {action.label}
                        </button>
                    ))}
                </div>
            )}

            <Can permission="invoice:share">
                <button type="button" onClick={() => onAction("share")}>
                    Share
                </button>
            </Can>
        </section>
    );
}

function InvoicePage({ invoiceId }: { invoiceId: string }) {
    const [selected, setSelected] = useState<string | null>(null);

    return (
        <>
            <InvoiceToolbar
                invoiceId={invoiceId}
                onAction={(actionId) => setSelected(actionId)}
            />
            {selected !== null && <p role="status">Selected action: {selected}</p>}
        </>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <InvoicePage invoiceId="INV-1042" />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. useAuthorization() derives the principal from the session user once per user object and memoizes the result, so can and hasRole keep a stable identity between renders — which is exactly what makes the useMemo above correct. Building the action list from data means a single filter decides visibility, an empty result degrades to an explanatory message instead of a broken toolbar, and role-based accents (hasRole("finance")) and one-off elements (Can) compose in the same component. Because the hook delegates to hasRole() and hasPermission() from blendsdk/authz, client checks use the same grant vocabulary the server issued.

Caveats and performance.

  • This is presentation only. The server is the authority; every action must also be enforced on the BFF endpoint.
  • Grants come from user.roles and user.permissions as untrusted runtime data. Non-array values, non-string entries, and duplicates are resolved fail-closed by the hook — but you should still not assume a claim exists.
  • can changes identity when the user object changes (a refresh that returns a new /me payload). Everything memoized on it recomputes, which is the desired behaviour.
  • Centralize permission strings so a typo is a compile error rather than a permanently hidden button:
tsx
export const INVOICE_PERMISSIONS = {
    write: "invoice:write",
    approve: "invoice:approve",
    delete: "invoice:delete",
    share: "invoice:share",
} as const;
  • Avoid calling can() inside a .map() over hundreds of rows on every render; filter once in a memo and render the result.

5. Scope Loader Ownership ​

When to use it. When two or more operations in the same screen can be in flight at once. The global loader is a single boolean, not a reference-counted stack: an operation that calls showLoader(false) hides the overlay for every other operation. Build a scope that counts active tasks and only clears the overlay when the last one finishes.

tsx
import {
    createContext,
    useCallback,
    useContext,
    useRef,
    useState,
    type ReactNode,
} from "react";
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

type LoaderTaskRunner = <T>(task: () => Promise<T>, text: string) => Promise<T>;

const LoaderScopeContext = createContext<LoaderTaskRunner | null>(null);

export function LoaderScope({ children }: { children: ReactNode }) {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();
    const activeTasks = useRef(0);

    const run = useCallback(
        async <T,>(task: () => Promise<T>, text: string): Promise<T> => {
            activeTasks.current += 1;
            if (activeTasks.current === 1) {
                setText(text);
                showLoader(true);
            }

            try {
                return await task();
            } finally {
                activeTasks.current -= 1;
                if (activeTasks.current === 0) {
                    showLoader(false);
                }
            }
        },
        [showLoader, setText],
    );

    return (
        <LoaderScopeContext.Provider value={run}>
            {children}
        </LoaderScopeContext.Provider>
    );
}

export function useLoaderTask(): LoaderTaskRunner {
    const run = useContext(LoaderScopeContext);
    if (run === null) {
        throw new Error("useLoaderTask() must be used within a <LoaderScope>.");
    }
    return run;
}

interface SyncResult {
    updated: number;
}

interface ExportResult {
    url: string;
}

function DataMaintenancePanel() {
    const runTask = useLoaderTask();
    const [status, setStatus] = useState("Idle");

    const sync = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            const result = await runTask(async () => {
                const response = await fetch("/api/maintenance/sync", { method: "POST" });
                if (!response.ok) {
                    throw new Error(`Sync failed with ${response.status}`);
                }
                const payload: SyncResult = await response.json();
                return payload;
            }, "Synchronizing records…");
            setStatus(`Updated ${result.updated} records`);
        } catch (caught) {
            setStatus(caught instanceof Error ? caught.message : "Sync failed");
        }
    };

    const createExport = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            const result = await runTask(async () => {
                const response = await fetch("/api/maintenance/export", { method: "POST" });
                if (!response.ok) {
                    throw new Error(`Export failed with ${response.status}`);
                }
                const payload: ExportResult = await response.json();
                return payload;
            }, "Preparing export…");
            setStatus(`Export ready: ${result.url}`);
        } catch (caught) {
            setStatus(caught instanceof Error ? caught.message : "Export failed");
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void sync()}>
                Synchronize
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void createExport()}>
                Export
            </button>
            <p role="status">{status}</p>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <LoaderScope>
                <DataMaintenancePanel />
            </LoaderScope>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. Loader bugs are race bugs: the overlay vanishes mid-request because a faster operation finished second. Counting active tasks inside one provider makes visibility a function of outstanding work rather than of call order, and finally guarantees the count is released on both success and failure. Mounting the counter in a provider — rather than a module-level variable or a per-component ref — means every consumer in the subtree shares the same count, while the scope still composes on top of the public useGlobalLoader() contract instead of reaching into the provider internals.

Caveats and performance.

  • The counter only knows about tasks routed through run. A raw showLoader(false) elsewhere in the tree still hides the overlay. Adopt the scope as the single way to drive the loader and treat direct calls as exceptional.
