  • The first task's text wins; the second concurrent task does not replace it. If you need changing messages, call setText inside run on every task and accept that the last writer wins.
  • showLoader(false) already clears the text, so the scope does not need a separate setText(null).
  • Do not start a task that outlives the provider and then expect the finally call to be meaningful; if GlobalLoaderProvider unmounts, there is no overlay left to hide. Abort in-flight work on unmount instead.
  • If a screen genuinely has one owner of the loading state — a single submit button, a single route transition — skip the scope. It is overhead when the simple boolean is already unambiguous.

6. Save Object-Shaped Form State Through the BFF ​

When to use it. A form with several related fields that must be validated, submitted with the CSRF token, and reset. Per-field useState makes the draft, validation, and reset drift apart:

tsx
const [customer, setCustomer] = useState("");
const [amount, setAmount] = useState("");
const [note, setNote] = useState("");
// three setters, three resets, three dependency entries

One object, one setter, one reset, one place to build the request body:

tsx
import { useState, type FormEvent } from "react";
import {
    AuthProvider,
    GlobalLoaderProvider,
    I18nProvider,
    useAuth,
    useGlobalLoader,
    useObjectState,
    useTranslations,
    type AuthConfig,
    type TranslationLoader,
} from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = { basePath: "/api/auth" };

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

interface InvoiceDraft {
    customer: string;
    amount: string;
    note: string;
}

function InvoiceForm() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    const { csrfToken, config } = useAuth();
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();
    const [draft, setDraft, resetDraft] = useObjectState<InvoiceDraft>(() => ({
        customer: "",
        amount: "",
        note: "",
    }));
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);
    const [saved, setSaved] = useState(false);

    const save = async (event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>): Promise<void> => {
        event.preventDefault();
        setError(null);
        setSaved(false);

        if (draft.customer.trim() === "") {
            setError(t("invoice.form.customerRequired"));
            return;
        }

        const amount = Number.parseFloat(draft.amount);
        if (!Number.isFinite(amount) || amount <= 0) {
            setError(t("invoice.form.amountInvalid"));
            return;
        }

        const headers: Record<string, string> = { "content-type": "application/json" };
        if (csrfToken !== null) {
            headers[config.csrfHeader] = csrfToken;
        }

        setText(t("invoice.form.saving"));
        showLoader(true);

        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/bff/invoices", {
                method: "POST",
                headers,
                body: JSON.stringify({
                    customer: draft.customer.trim(),
                    amount,
                    note: draft.note,
                }),
            });

            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(t("invoice.form.saveFailed", { status: response.status }));
            }

            resetDraft();
            setSaved(true);
        } catch (caught) {
            setError(
                caught instanceof Error
                    ? caught.message
                    : t("invoice.form.unexpectedError"),
            );
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={(event) => void save(event)}>
            <label>
                {t("invoice.form.customer")}
                <input
                    value={draft.customer}
                    onChange={(event) => setDraft({ customer: event.target.value })}
                />
            </label>

            <label>
                {t("invoice.form.amount")}
                <input
                    inputMode="decimal"
                    value={draft.amount}
                    onChange={(event) => setDraft({ amount: event.target.value })}
                />
            </label>

            <label>
                {t("invoice.form.note")}
                <textarea
                    value={draft.note}
                    onChange={(event) => setDraft({ note: event.target.value })}
                />
            </label>

            {error !== null && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
            {saved && <p role="status">{t("invoice.form.saved")}</p>}

            <button type="submit">{t("invoice.form.submit")}</button>
            <button type="button" onClick={resetDraft}>
                {t("common.reset")}
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
                    <InvoiceForm />
                </AuthProvider>
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. The draft is a single value, so validation reads one object, the request body is built from the same object, and resetDraft() restores every field at once — the reset baseline is a fresh object produced by the factory, not the initial reference. The raw amount string is kept in state and parsed only at the boundary, which avoids rendering NaN into a controlled input while still sending a number to the BFF. The submit path combines all four modules in the order they exist at runtime: t() for field labels and errors, csrfToken/config.csrfHeader for the mutation, showLoader/setText for progress, and the object setter for the draft.

Caveats and performance.

  • showLoader(false) in finally makes this form the single owner of the overlay during submit. If other work can run concurrently, route the submit through the loader scope from pattern 5 instead.
  • setDraft shallow-merges, so nested structures are replaced wholesale. Keep InvoiceDraft flat, or replace the nested object explicitly.
  • reset() re-runs the factory captured on the first render. If the initial values must come from props, they will not update after mount; key the component to remount when the source changes.
  • The direct fetch here is deliberate to keep the example self-contained. In a real application, submit through the client from pattern 3 so error handling and header logic are shared.
  • Translation keys are evaluated during submit. If the screen must not render before translations are ready, gate the route on ready in the provider composition from pattern 1.

7. Renew an Expiring Session ​

When to use it. Long-lived screens — editors, wizards, dashboards — where a session expiring mid-task would lose work. With autoRefresh enabled the provider already renews before expiry; this pattern surfaces the remaining time and gives the user an explicit recovery path when the automatic refresh fails or is disabled.

tsx
import { useEffect, useState } from "react";
import {
    AuthProvider,
    GlobalLoaderProvider,
    I18nProvider,
    useAuth,
    useTranslations,
    type AuthConfig,
    type TranslationLoader,
} from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    autoRefresh: true,
    refreshLeadTime: 60,
};

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

const WARNING_THRESHOLD_SECONDS = 300;

function useSecondsUntilExpiry(): number | null {
    const { expiresAt } = useAuth();
    const [secondsLeft, setSecondsLeft] = useState<number | null>(null);

    useEffect(() => {
        if (expiresAt === null) {
            setSecondsLeft(null);
            return;
        }

        const compute = (): void => {
            const remaining = Math.floor(expiresAt - Date.now() / 1000);
            setSecondsLeft(Math.max(0, remaining));
        };

        compute();
        const timer = window.setInterval(compute, 1000);
        return () => window.clearInterval(timer);
    }, [expiresAt]);

    return secondsLeft;
}

function SessionExpiryBanner() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    const { isAuthenticated, isLoading, refresh, login } = useAuth();
    const secondsLeft = useSecondsUntilExpiry();
    const [refreshFailed, setRefreshFailed] = useState(false);

    if (
        isLoading ||
        !isAuthenticated ||
        secondsLeft === null ||
        secondsLeft > WARNING_THRESHOLD_SECONDS
    ) {
        return null;
    }

    const staySignedIn = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setRefreshFailed(false);
        try {
            const refreshed = await refresh();
            if (!refreshed) {
                setRefreshFailed(true);
            }
        } catch {
            setRefreshFailed(true);
        }
    };

    const signInAgain = (): void => {
        login(window.location.pathname + window.location.search);
    };

    if (secondsLeft === 0) {
        return (
            <div role="alert">
                <p>{t("session.expired")}</p>
                <button type="button" onClick={signInAgain}>
                    {t("session.signInAgain")}
                </button>
            </div>
        );
    }

    return (
        <div role="status">
            <p>{t("session.expiresIn", { seconds: secondsLeft })}</p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void staySignedIn()}>
                {t("session.staySignedIn")}
            </button>
            {refreshFailed && (
                <p role="alert">
                    {t("session.refreshFailed")}{" "}
                    <button type="button" onClick={signInAgain}>
                        {t("session.signInAgain")}
                    </button>
                </p>
            )}
        </div>
    );
}

function Dashboard() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    const { user } = useAuth();

    return <h1>{t("dashboard.welcome", { name: user?.sub ?? "guest" })}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
                    <SessionExpiryBanner />
                    <Dashboard />
                </AuthProvider>
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why it matters. expiresAt is a Unix timestamp in seconds, so the remaining time can be recomputed from the clock instead of decremented — the display cannot drift, and a refresh that returns a new expiry automatically restarts the countdown through the effect dependency. refresh() resolves to a boolean rather than throwing, so failure is an ordinary branch: retry with the manual button, or fall back to login(returnTo) with the current path so the user returns to the same screen after the OIDC round-trip. Every string is translated, which lets the banner sit in the same i18n subtree as the rest of the shell.

Caveats and performance.

  • Mount the banner once, near the root. Each instance runs its own one-second interval; several copies add timers without adding information.
  • autoRefresh already performs renewal refreshLeadTime seconds before expiry. Treat the banner as visibility plus manual recovery, not as a replacement for automatic refresh. If you disable autoRefresh, this becomes the primary renewal path.
  • Never call login() during render — it navigates. Call it from an event handler, as shown.
  • expiresAt is null when the server did not report an expiry; the hook then renders nothing rather than inventing a countdown.
  • A refresh() that succeeds updates the auth context on the next render. Components that read csrfToken directly keep the previous token until then, so do not pair this pattern with a synchronous retry that assumes the new token is already available.
  • Overlapping refreshes are possible if the automatic schedule fires while the user also presses the button. The provider serializes its own refresh logic, but guard against double-clicks locally if the operation is expensive.

Choosing a Pattern ​

ProblemPatternModules involved
Providers are mounted in different places, or in the wrong order1Loader, I18n, auth
Content flashes before /me resolves, or pages call login() during render2Auth, guards
Mutations intermittently fail with 4033Auth, fetch
Permission strings are scattered through JSX4Authorization
The overlay disappears while work is still running5Loader
A form has one useState per field and three reset paths6State, auth, I18n, loader
Users lose work when the session expires7Auth, I18n

Rules That Hold Across All Patterns ​

  • The server is the authority. Every client-side check in this document — AuthGuard, RequireAccess, Can, useAuthorization() — is presentation. The BFF must enforce the same rules on every endpoint.
  • Hooks throw outside their provider. useGlobalLoader, useTranslations, useAuth, and useAuthorization fail with a descriptive error when the provider is missing. The useLoaderTask() hook in pattern 5 follows the same convention; any new capability you build on top of these primitives should too.
  • The loader is a boolean, not a stack. Either give a workflow one owner (patterns 6 and 7) or route every task through a counting scope (pattern 5). Mixing both reintroduces the race.
  • The CSRF token is a snapshot. It can be rotated by the server and is only as fresh as the last /me or /refresh. Treat 403 on a mutation as a possible stale-token outcome, not automatically as a permission bug.
  • Configuration is captured on mount. GlobalLoaderProvider appearance and AuthProvider endpoint resolution are fixed for the lifetime of the provider. Changing either requires a remount.
  • useObjectState is provider-independent. It composes with every pattern here but depends on none of them; keep its state flat and its factory pure.

react Best Practices ​

blendsdk/react is infrastructure, not a component kit: providers own the session, the translation catalog, and the loading overlay, while hooks read that state from React context. Most mistakes with this package are therefore behavioral rather than syntactic — a session that is re-checked on every navigation, an overlay that never hides, an authorization check that renders the wrong thing, or object state that silently stops updating.

Each practice below is presented as a pair: the failing pattern first, then the recommended one, followed by the consequence of getting it wrong. The rules apply to all four modules — auth, authorization, i18n, and object state — and to provider composition across them.

ConcernDoDon't
Provider placementMount providers once, above the router and every consumerMount providers inside route components or conditionals
Provider compositionMount I18nProvider inside GlobalLoaderProviderMount the i18n provider outside the loader
AuthenticationDistinguish isAuthenticated from authorized; wait for isLoadingTreat a present user as server authorization
Auth pathsSet loginPath for the frontend route; keep endpoints.login for the BFFUse endpoints.login as a frontend route
Auth actionsawait logout() and inspect the boolean from refresh()Fire-and-forget promises and ignore failure
CSRFSend csrfToken under config.csrfHeaderHard-code x-csrf-token or send empty tokens
AuthorizationUse useAuthorization() for grantsRead or cast raw user.roles / user.permissions
Global loaderClear it in finally; one owner per visible periodLeave it visible on errors; run overlapping operations
I18nGate translated UI on ready; call setLocale() from eventsRender t() before load; call setLocale() during render
Object stateFunctional patches, immutable updates, pure factoryStale patches, in-place mutation, shared baseline objects

Do / Don't Pairs ​

Mount providers once, above every consumer ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionBar() {
    const { user } = useAuth();
    return <span>{user?.sub ?? "anonymous"}</span>;
}

export function DashboardRoute() {
    // ❌ The provider is route-local: navigating away unmounts it, and every
    // return discards the session state and re-runs the initial /me check.
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SessionBar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionBar() {
    const { user } = useAuth();
    return <span>{user?.sub ?? "anonymous"}</span>;
}

function DashboardRoute() {
    return <SessionBar />;
}

export function App() {
    // ✅ Mounted once at the root, outside route transitions.
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <DashboardRoute />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. AuthProvider hydrates the session from GET {basePath}/me on mount and schedules automatic renewal. A provider mounted inside a route component unmounts whenever that route leaves the tree, so the next visit restarts the session check and re-fetches /me. During that window isLoading is true again, and any guard or UI that reacts to authentication state briefly sees an empty session. Hoist providers above the router; render routes and guards inside.

Mount I18nProvider inside GlobalLoaderProvider ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Title() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    return <h1>{t("app.title")}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        // ❌ I18nProvider reports translation fetches through the global
        // loader, but the loader is mounted below it here.
        <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
            <GlobalLoaderProvider>
                <Title />
            </GlobalLoaderProvider>
        </I18nProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Title() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    return <h1>{t("app.title")}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        // ✅ Global loader outermost, translations inside it.
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <Title />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why. The i18n provider uses the global loader while fetching translations. When it is mounted outside GlobalLoaderProvider, its internal loader call has no context to consume and fails at the first translation load. The supported composition is outside in: GlobalLoaderProvider → I18nProvider → AuthProvider → routes and guards. Only the loader/i18n edge is mandatory; the auth subtree may sit inside or outside i18n depending on whether auth screens need translations.

Separate isAuthenticated from authorized ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoicePage() {
    const { user, isAuthenticated } = useAuth();

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
        return <p>Please sign in.</p>;
    }

    // ❌ A user object only means the session exists. The BFF can still have
    // denied the session, in which case authorized === false and this renders
    // data the server has refused.
    return <h1>Invoices for {user?.sub}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoicePage />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoicePage() {
    const { user, isAuthenticated, isLoading, authorized } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated || user === null) {
        return <p>Please sign in.</p>;
    }

    if (!authorized) {
        return <p>Your account is not authorized to view invoices.</p>;
    }

    return <h1>Invoices for {user.sub}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoicePage />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. The two flags answer different questions. isAuthenticated is derived from user !== null; authorized is the server's decision for the session. A signed-in user can be authenticated and unauthorized at the same time, and authorized is also false before the first /me check, for anonymous or failed checks, and after logout. Checking isLoading first prevents the first render from showing a false "not authorized" state.

Keep loginPath and endpoints.login distinct ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    // ❌ The sign-in page lives at /sign-in, so the login endpoint is
    // overridden. But endpoints.login is the BFF route: login() now
    // navigates to /api/auth/sign-in, and AuthGuard still redirects to
    // the default frontend route /login.
    endpoints: { login: "/sign-in" },
};

function Dashboard() {
    return <h1>Dashboard</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <Dashboard />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { AuthProvider } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    // ✅ Frontend route used by AuthGuard for its redirect.
    loginPath: "/sign-in",
    // ✅ endpoints.login keeps its default: the BFF route /api/auth/login
    // that login() navigates to.
};

function Dashboard() {
    return <h1>Dashboard</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <Dashboard />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. login() navigates to ${basePath}${endpoints.login}, which is a backend route; AuthGuard redirects to loginPath, which is a frontend route. They serve different layers and can legitimately have different values. Overriding the wrong one either sends the browser to a missing BFF endpoint or redirects users to a frontend page that does not exist. Set both deliberately and never put an absolute URL in endpoints; those paths are relative to basePath.

Await logout() and surface failures ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SignOutButton() {
    const { logout } = useAuth();

    // ❌ The promise is dropped. If the logout request fails, the failure is
    // unhandled, the user stays signed in, and the UI gives no feedback.
    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => { void logout(); }}>
            Sign out
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SignOutButton />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SignOutButton() {
    const { logout } = useAuth();
    const [error, setError] = useState<string | null>(null);

    const handleSignOut = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setError(null);
        try {
            await logout();
        } catch (cause) {
            setError(cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : "Sign out failed.");
        }
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleSignOut()}>
                Sign out
            </button>
            {error !== null && <p role="alert">{error}</p>}
        </div>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SignOutButton />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. logout() is asynchronous: it calls the BFF logout endpoint and then clears local state. Dropping the promise hides a failed logout from both the user and the console. Awaiting the call lets you show progress, keep the user informed on failure, and avoid navigating away before the session is actually cleared.

Check the boolean returned by refresh() ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function RefreshButton() {
    const { refresh } = useAuth();

    // ❌ refresh() resolves to false when the session could not be renewed.
    // Ignoring the result treats a failed refresh as a success.
    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => { void refresh(); }}>
            Refresh session
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <RefreshButton />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { useState } from "react";
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function RefreshButton() {
    const { refresh } = useAuth();
    const [status, setStatus] = useState<string | null>(null);

    const handleRefresh = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            const renewed = await refresh();
            setStatus(renewed ? "Session renewed." : "Session could not be renewed.");
        } catch (cause) {
            setStatus(cause instanceof Error ? cause.message : "Refresh failed.");
        }
    };

    return (
        <div>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleRefresh()}>
                Refresh session
            </button>
            {status !== null && <p role="status">{status}</p>}
        </div>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <RefreshButton />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. Manual refresh reports failure through its boolean result, not only through exceptions. The provider already schedules renewal when autoRefresh is enabled, so this button should exist for explicit user action or recovery, never as a replacement for the schedule. Polling refresh() on a timer duplicates the built-in renewal and can race it.

Send the CSRF token under the configured header ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function DeleteInvoiceButton({ invoiceId }: { invoiceId: string }) {
    const { csrfToken } = useAuth();

    const handleDelete = async (): Promise<void> => {
        // ❌ Hard-codes the default header name and sends an empty value when
        // CSRF is not enforced (csrfToken === null).
        await fetch(`/api/bff/invoices/${invoiceId}`, {
            method: "DELETE",
            headers: { "x-csrf-token": csrfToken ?? "" },
        });
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleDelete()}>
            Delete invoice
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <DeleteInvoiceButton invoiceId="42" />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function DeleteInvoiceButton({ invoiceId }: { invoiceId: string }) {
    const { csrfToken, config } = useAuth();

    const handleDelete = async (): Promise<void> => {
        const headers: Record<string, string> = {};
        if (csrfToken !== null) {
            headers[config.csrfHeader] = csrfToken;
        }

        try {
            const response = await fetch(`/api/bff/invoices/${invoiceId}`, {
                method: "DELETE",
                headers,
            });
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Delete failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (cause) {
            console.error("Could not delete invoice", cause);
        }
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleDelete()}>
            Delete invoice
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <DeleteInvoiceButton invoiceId="42" />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. The server decides which header carries the token; csrfHeader is configurable precisely because deployments differ, and the default x-csrf-token is only a default. Hard-coding the header breaks those deployments. When csrfToken is null, CSRF is not enforced, and sending an empty header can be rejected rather than ignored. Send the token only to same-origin BFF calls and only when it exists.

Use useAuthorization() instead of reading raw claims ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceToolbar() {
    const { user } = useAuth();

    // ❌ user.roles is `unknown`. The assertion hides missing or malformed
    // claims, and the expression crashes when the value is not an array.
    const roles = user?.roles as string[];

    return <p>Roles: {roles?.join(", ") ?? "none"}</p>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoiceToolbar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuthorization } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceToolbar() {
    const { roles, permissions, hasRole, can } = useAuthorization();

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Roles: {roles.length > 0 ? roles.join(", ") : "none"}</p>
            <p>Permissions: {permissions.length > 0 ? permissions.join(", ") : "none"}</p>
            {hasRole("finance") && <strong>Finance</strong>}
            {can("invoice:write") && <button type="button">Edit invoice</button>}
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoiceToolbar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Why. Session claims are untrusted runtime data: user.roles and user.permissions are typed as unknown, may be absent, may not be arrays, and may contain non-string entries. A cast moves that failure into render. useAuthorization() sanitizes the claims — non-arrays become empty lists, non-string entries are ignored, duplicates are removed — and returns an empty principal for anonymous users, so requirements fail closed. Its result is also memoized on the user, keeping hasRole and can stable between renders.

Clear the global loader in finally ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function SaveButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();

    const handleSave = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Saving…");
        showLoader(true);

        // ❌ If the request rejects, the overlay is never hidden and blocks
        // the entire application.
        await fetch("/api/invoices/42", { method: "PUT" });
        showLoader(false);
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleSave()}>
            Save
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <SaveButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function SaveButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();

    const handleSave = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Saving…");
        showLoader(true);
        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/invoices/42", { method: "PUT" });
            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Save failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (cause) {
            console.error("Could not save invoice", cause);
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleSave()}>
            Save
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <SaveButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why. The overlay is full-screen and blocks interaction; leaving it visible on the error path makes the application unusable until a reload. showLoader(false) also clears the text, so the finally block handles both cleanup steps. Set the text while the loader is visible, and avoid setting it after hiding it.

Give each visible loader period a single owner ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceLoader() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();

    const load = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Loading invoices…");
        showLoader(true);
        await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
            setTimeout(() => resolve(), 400);
        });
        showLoader(false);
    };

    return <button type="button" onClick={() => void load()}>Load invoices</button>;
}

function ReportLoader() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();

    const load = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Building report…");
        showLoader(true);
        await new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
            setTimeout(() => resolve(), 800);
        });
        showLoader(false);
    };

    return <button type="button" onClick={() => void load()}>Build report</button>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        // ❌ Two components control one visibility flag. The faster operation
        // hides the overlay while the slower one is still running.
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <InvoiceLoader />
            <ReportLoader />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function WorkflowPanel() {
    const { showLoader, setText } = useGlobalLoader();

    const runBoth = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Working…");
        showLoader(true);
        try {
            await Promise.all([
                new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
                    setTimeout(() => resolve(), 400);
                }),
                new Promise<void>((resolve) => {
                    setTimeout(() => resolve(), 800);
                }),
            ]);
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return <button type="button" onClick={() => void runBoth()}>Run both</button>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        // ✅ One component owns the visible period.
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <WorkflowPanel />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why. The loader is a single visible boolean, not a reference-counted stack. Every showLoader(false) hides the overlay for all operations, and every setText overwrites the shared message. Independent widgets should use local loading indicators; the global overlay is for coarse operations owned by one component that starts and finishes them together.

Gate translated UI on ready ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Header() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();

    // ❌ Translations load asynchronously; the first render happens before the
    // catalog exists, so translated text cannot be displayed yet.
    return <h1>{t("app.title")}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <Header />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Header() {
    const { t, ready } = useTranslations();

    if (!ready) {
        // ✅ Stable fallback until the catalog is available.
        return <h1 aria-busy="true">Loading translations…</h1>;
    }

    return <h1>{t("app.title")}</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <Header />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why. I18nProvider loads the default locale on mount; until that load succeeds, ready is false and the catalog is not available to t(). Rendering translated text unconditionally produces an untranslated first paint and unnecessary layout shifts. Gate the components that need translations, not unrelated static UI.

Change the locale from an event, never during render ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function LocaleSwitcher() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale } = useTranslations();

    // ❌ Calling setLocale during render triggers a loader fetch and a state
    // update on every render, which can loop indefinitely.
    setLocale(locale === "en" ? "nl" : "en");

    return <button type="button">{t("language.switch")}</button>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <LocaleSwitcher />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function LocaleSwitcher() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale } = useTranslations();

    const toggleLocale = (): void => {
        setLocale(locale === "en" ? "nl" : "en");
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={toggleLocale}>
            {t("language.switch")}
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <LocaleSwitcher />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

Why. setLocale() is an action, not a value: it changes provider state and triggers a new loader call. React renders must stay pure; calling it during render updates the provider while rendering and re-triggers the same code, which can loop and fire a fetch per render. Call it from a click handler, or from an effect when syncing the locale to a route parameter.

Use functional patches when the next value depends on the previous ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface CounterState {
    count: number;
    lastAction: string;
}

export function Counter() {
    const [state, setState] = useObjectState<CounterState>(() => ({
        count: 0,
        lastAction: "reset",
    }));

    const incrementTwice = (): void => {
        // ❌ Both patches are computed from the same render value. The second
        // write replaces the first, so count grows by one instead of two.
        setState({ count: state.count + 1, lastAction: "increment" });
        setState({ count: state.count + 1, lastAction: "increment" });
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={incrementTwice}>
            Count: {state.count}
        </button>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface CounterState {
    count: number;
    lastAction: string;
}

export function Counter() {
    const [state, setState] = useObjectState<CounterState>(() => ({
        count: 0,
        lastAction: "reset",
    }));

    const incrementTwice = (): void => {
        // ✅ Each functional update receives the latest state.
        setState((previous) => ({
            count: previous.count + 1,
            lastAction: "increment",
        }));
        setState((previous) => ({
            count: previous.count + 1,
            lastAction: "increment",
        }));
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={incrementTwice}>
            Count: {state.count}
        </button>
    );
}

Why. The setter applies a patch to the latest state internally, but the patch expression itself is evaluated when the call is made. Building the patch from state captured at render means consecutive updates all start from the same baseline, and the last one wins. The functional form moves the calculation inside React's updater, where previous is the latest state.

Treat object state as immutable and flat ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface FilterState {
    query: string;
    statuses: string[];
}

export function InvoiceFilters() {
    const [filters, setFilters] = useObjectState<FilterState>(() => ({
        query: "",
        statuses: [],
    }));

    const addStatus = (status: string): void => {
        // ❌ Mutating the stored array keeps the same state object: no setter
        // call means no re-render, and the reset baseline can be polluted.
        filters.statuses.push(status);
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => addStatus("open")}>
            {filters.statuses.join(", ") || "No filters"}
        </button>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface FilterState {
    query: string;
    statuses: string[];
}

export function InvoiceFilters() {
    const [filters, setFilters] = useObjectState<FilterState>(() => ({
        query: "",
        statuses: [],
    }));

    const addStatus = (status: string): void => {
        // ✅ Replace the array and send it through the setter.
        setFilters((previous) => ({
            statuses: [...previous.statuses, status],
        }));
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => addStatus("open")}>
            {filters.statuses.join(", ") || "No filters"}
        </button>
    );
}

Why. The hook detects updates only when the setter is called; in-place mutation keeps the same object reference and React has nothing to schedule. Replacement also preserves the reset contract. The hook is built for plain objects: top-level arrays and class instances are outside the contract because object spreading drops array behavior and prototypes. Nested objects are replaced, not deep-merged, so spread them yourself when updating a nested field. Setting a property to undefined leaves the key present; model optional properties explicitly instead of using undefined as a delete.

Return a fresh object from the useObjectState factory ​

❌ Wrong

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface Settings {
    theme: "light" | "dark";
    notifications: boolean;
}

// ❌ Every factory call returns the same object reference.
const sharedDefaults: Settings = { theme: "light", notifications: true };

export function SettingsEditor() {
    const [settings, setSettings, reset] = useObjectState<Settings>(() => sharedDefaults);

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Theme: {settings.theme}</p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => setSettings({ theme: "dark" })}>
                Use dark theme
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={reset}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

✅ Correct

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface Settings {
    theme: "light" | "dark";
    notifications: boolean;
}

// ✅ A new plain object on every call, so state never aliases the baseline.
const createDefaults = (): Settings => ({
    theme: "light",
    notifications: true,
});

export function SettingsEditor() {
    const [settings, setSettings, reset] = useObjectState<Settings>(createDefaults);

    return (
        <div>
            <p>Theme: {settings.theme}</p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => setSettings({ theme: "dark" })}>
                Use dark theme
            </button>
            <button type="button" onClick={reset}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </div>
    );
}

Why. The factory runs lazily on mount, may run twice in development StrictMode, and runs again on every reset(). If it returns a shared object, the state and the reset baseline alias the same reference; any in-place mutation leaks into every reset, and later mounts observe mutated defaults. The factory must be pure and return a new plain object each time. It is captured on the first render, so changing the create argument later does not change the reset baseline.

Anti-Patterns ​

Using client-side authorization as the security boundary ​

Can, RequireAccess, hasRole(), and can() decide what the UI renders. They are not enforcement: React code is visible to users, requests can be issued outside the application, and every client check can be bypassed. The BFF must reject the same operation when the grant is missing. A hidden button is a convenience; a rejected request is the actual control.

typescript
const { can } = useAuthorization();
const mayEdit = can("invoice:write");
// Render the control only when mayEdit is true — but the API must still
// return 403 when the caller lacks invoice:write.

Calling provider hooks from non-React code ​

useAuth(), useAuthorization(), useTranslations(), useGlobalLoader(), and useObjectState() are React hooks: they must be called from a component or another hook during render. Calling them from a utility function, an event bus, a route loader, or a module-level initializer either violates the rules of hooks or throws because the context is only available inside the provider subtree. Read the value in a component and pass it to the utility, or wrap the logic in a custom hook.

Building a parallel auth client ​

Manually fetching /me, storing the user in another store, and scheduling your own refresh timer duplicates the provider and drifts from it. AuthProvider is the only thing maintaining user, authorized, expiresAt, and csrfToken; a second client will miss session changes, double the refresh calls, and disagree with the guards. Consume useAuth() instead.

Storing tokens in browser storage ​

The auth model is a BFF session: tokens stay on the server and the browser holds an HttpOnly cookie that JavaScript cannot read. Do not copy tokens into localStorage or sessionStorage, and do not try to read the session cookie through document.cookie. If a feature appears to need the token in the browser, move the call to the BFF.

Expecting provider configuration to update at runtime ​

GlobalLoaderConfig is captured on mount and is not reactive; AuthConfig is merged with AUTH_DEFAULTS on mount and exposed as the resolved useAuth().config. Re-rendering the provider with a new object does not apply the change. Treat both as static startup configuration. If a change is genuinely required, remount the provider with a new key — and accept that everything below it remounts as well.

Running overlapping global-loader operations ​

The loader is one visibility flag and one message, not a per-operation tracker. Two widgets that call showLoader(true) and later showLoader(false) will hide the overlay for each other, and setText is last-writer-wins. Give each visible period one owner, or keep per-widget progress local to the widget.

Hard-coding the CSRF header or treating the token as permanent ​

The token is exposed as csrfToken and the header name as config.csrfHeader; use both. Hard-coding x-csrf-token breaks when the server uses a different header. Caching the token in a module variable ignores rotation: the token can be regenerated when session-id rotation is enabled, and another browsing context can replace it without this tab observing the change until the next session check. On a 403 caused by an outdated token, await refresh() and retry once instead of dropping CSRF protection.

Using absolute URLs in endpoint overrides ​

endpoints paths are relative to basePath; the provider concatenates them. An absolute URL or a path outside basePath produces a wrong navigation target and can leak the CSRF token to another origin if the resulting request is cross-origin. Keep basePath and all endpoint overrides same-origin and application-controlled.

Mounting nested or duplicate providers ​

A second AuthProvider in a subtree creates a second session, a second /me request, and a second refresh schedule. Consumers inside see the nearest provider, while consumers outside see the outer one, so the application silently operates with two authentication states. Mount each provider once at the root; split layouts instead of re-wrapping subtrees.

Using redirect guards for element visibility ​

AuthGuard and RequireAccess redirect; they are route-level gates. Wrapping a button or toolbar in a redirecting guard navigates the user away when the condition fails instead of hiding the control. Use Can or useAuthorization() for elements, and reserve the guards for routes.

Overloading isLoading as a general loading flag ​

isLoading covers only the initial session check. It does not track refresh(), logout(), or any application request. Using it as a global spinner flag produces a loader that never reflects the actual operation. Keep separate state for other async work, or use the global loader deliberately.

Performance Tips ​

  1. Hoist providers to avoid re-hydration. Every AuthProvider mount performs the /me check and schedules renewal; every I18nProvider mount fetches translations. Mounting providers above the router means route changes cost neither network round-trips nor session-state resets. A keyed remount for loader theming should be a deliberate, rare operation because it remounts the entire subtree.

  2. Keep context consumers local. A context value change re-renders every component that consumes that context. Reading useAuth() once in a top-level layout and passing user down re-renders the layout and its children on every session change; reading useAuth() in the leaf components that actually display the user narrows the render to those leaves. Apply the same rule to useGlobalLoader(): it should be called by the component that owns the operation, not by every row in a list, because every message change re-renders all consumers.

  3. Let autoRefresh do the scheduling. With autoRefresh enabled (the default), the provider refreshes once per expiry window at expiresAt - refreshLeadTime. A manual interval adds duplicate requests, can race the scheduled refresh, and multiplies server load across open tabs. Use refresh() for explicit user action or recovery, not as a polling loop.

  4. Reuse the memoized authorization result. useAuthorization() memoizes on user, so roles, permissions, hasRole, and can stay referentially stable between session updates. Deriving a filtered roles array or a permission Set inside render creates new objects every time and defeats memoized children. Pass the predicates or the booleans they produce.

  5. Group related fields in useObjectState, but keep the object small. One state cell for a form avoids a useState call per field and updates the whole form with one render. Each patch still copies the top-level object, so do not store large server collections there; keep lists in their own state and derive expensive values with useMemo instead of storing them.

  6. Use the global loader for coarse work only. Showing the overlay blocks the entire application and causes a full-screen paint; toggling it for every fetch produces flicker and blocks unrelated interactions. Per-widget progress belongs in the widget; a single overlay is for route transitions, session bootstrap, and save operations that must prevent interaction.

  7. Call setLocale() only when the locale actually changes. Each call triggers a new loader invocation. Avoid binding it to inputs that fire per keystroke; a select or button is sufficient. If translations are served over HTTP, let the loader benefit from caching headers or an ETag rather than refetching unchanged catalogs.

  8. Skip the router dependency when you do not redirect. react-router is an optional peer needed only by AuthGuard and RequireAccess. Applications that use Can, useAuthorization(), and the other hooks never import it, so the bundler omits it. Importing a guard just for convenience pulls the router into the bundle.

  9. Pass the stable useObjectState callbacks directly. setState and reset keep the same identity across renders. Passing them to memoized children is safe without an extra useCallback wrapper, and the wrapper itself would create a new dependency object for no benefit.

Security Considerations ​

  1. The server is the authorization boundary. Can, RequireAccess, hasRole(), can(), and authorized decide rendering. Every endpoint must independently enforce the same grants; client code is readable, modifiable, and bypassable. Treat UI gating as a usability feature, never as the control that protects data.

  2. Tokens never enter JavaScript. The BFF keeps access and refresh tokens server-side and gives the browser an HttpOnly session cookie. Do not store tokens in localStorage or sessionStorage, do not attempt to read the session cookie via document.cookie, and do not expose tokens through your own endpoints. If the client appears to need a token, move the call that needs it to the BFF.

  3. Send CSRF tokens on state-changing calls. Read csrfToken and config.csrfHeader from useAuth() and send the header on POST, PUT, PATCH, and DELETE requests to the BFF. Send it only to same-origin endpoints. When a request is rejected with 403 because the token rotated, await refresh() to obtain the current token and retry once; do not disable CSRF or fall back to an unauthenticated call.

  4. Prevent open redirects through returnTo. login(returnTo?) and defaultReturnTo become navigation targets. Never pass window.location.href, a query parameter, or any other user-controlled string without validating that it is an internal path. Reject protocol-relative and backslash-containing values, which browsers may normalize into external URLs.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function toInternalPath(candidate: string): string {
    if (!candidate.startsWith("/") || candidate.startsWith("//") || candidate.includes("\\")) {
        return "/";
    }
    return candidate;
}

function SignInLink({ next }: { next: string }) {
    const { login } = useAuth();

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => login(toInternalPath(next))}>
            Sign in
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth", defaultReturnTo: "/" }}>
            <SignInLink next="/invoices" />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

  1. Treat claims and translations as untrusted data. AuthUser is typed with [key: string]: unknown; do not cast a claim to a trusted type without validating it. Render claims and t() results as text — React escapes string children — and never pass them to dangerouslySetInnerHTML. Interpolation is not sanitization; translation values are data, not HTML.

  2. Recognize that session snapshots go stale. authorized, expiresAt, and csrfToken reflect the last /me or refresh response. Another tab can sign out, replace the session, or rotate the CSRF token without this tab observing it. Privileged operations must revalidate on the server, and the client should handle 401 and 403 by refreshing or re-checking the session instead of assuming the previous flag still holds.

  3. Trust the configuration source. basePath and endpoint overrides determine where the browser is sent for login and where the CSRF token is transmitted. Keep them in static application configuration, same-origin, and out of user input. A manipulated basePath redirects the login flow and can expose the token to an attacker-controlled host.

  4. Do not log credentials or full claims. Avoid logging csrfToken, raw /me responses, or complete user objects in production error reporting. Log the failure and a non-sensitive identifier such as user.sub, and redact the rest.

react Common Scenarios ​

This document answers common implementation questions with complete, runnable examples. All examples import from the public blendsdk/react entry point, use React 19 function components, and follow strict TypeScript conventions.

How do I compose the providers for an application? ​

Solution: Mount GlobalLoaderProvider outermost, then I18nProvider, then AuthProvider. The I18n provider uses the global loader while fetching translations, so it must sit inside GlobalLoaderProvider. AuthProvider can sit inside or outside the I18n subtree depending on whether auth UI needs translations. useObjectState requires no provider.

ProviderResponsibilityRequired by
GlobalLoaderProviderFull-screen loading overlayuseGlobalLoader, I18nProvider
I18nProviderTranslation loading and t()useTranslations
AuthProviderBFF session, actions, CSRF tokenuseAuth, useAuthorization, auth guards
tsx
import { AuthProvider, GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function Application() {
    return <main>BlendSDK application</main>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
                    <Application />
                </AuthProvider>
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I show a global loading overlay during an async operation? ​

Solution: Call setText() and showLoader(true) before the operation, and clear the loader in a finally block. showLoader(false) also clears the message. The loader is a single visibility flag, not a reference-counted stack, so overlapping operations share the same overlay.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function SaveInvoiceButton() {
    const { showLoader, setText, visible } = useGlobalLoader();

    const save = async (): Promise<void> => {
        setText("Saving invoice…");
        showLoader(true);

        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/invoices/42", {
                method: "PUT",
                headers: { "content-type": "application/json" },
                body: JSON.stringify({ status: "sent" }),
            });

            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Save failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not save invoice", error);
        } finally {
            showLoader(false);
        }
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void save()} disabled={visible}>
            {visible ? "Saving…" : "Save invoice"}
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <SaveInvoiceButton />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I customize the global loader's spinner and message? ​

Solution: Pass a GlobalLoaderConfig to GlobalLoaderProvider. All properties are optional. The configuration is captured on mount and is not reactive, so changing it requires remounting the provider. Use textComponent to replace the default message renderer.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, useGlobalLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

function LoaderPreview() {
    const { showLoader, setText, visible } = useGlobalLoader();

    const preview = (): void => {
        setText("Preparing your workspace…");
        showLoader(true);
        window.setTimeout(() => {
            showLoader(false);
        }, 1500);
    };

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={preview} disabled={visible}>
            Preview loader
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider
            config={{
                spinnerColor: "#25b09b",
                spinnerWidth: 4,
                spinnerSize: 64,
                backgroundColor: "rgba(15, 23, 42, 0.35)",
                textColor: "#f8fafc",
                zIndex: 1000000,
                textComponent: ({ text, textColor }) => (
                    <span style={{ color: textColor, fontWeight: 600 }}>{text}</span>
                ),
            }}
        >
            <LoaderPreview />
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I load translations from an API? ​

Solution: Supply a TranslationLoader to I18nProvider. The provider calls it for the default locale on mount and exposes the result through t(). Use ready to avoid rendering untranslated UI. If the loader rejects, the provider exposes no public error field; catch failures inside the loader or surface them through an error boundary.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function WelcomePanel() {
    const { t, ready } = useTranslations();

    if (!ready) {
        return <p>Loading translations…</p>;
    }

    return (
        <section>
            <h1>{t("dashboard.title")}</h1>
            <p>{t("dashboard.welcome", { name: "Ada" })}</p>
            <p>{t("cart.items", { count: 3 })}</p>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <WelcomePanel />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I change the active locale or reload translations at runtime? ​

Solution: setLocale(locale) switches the language and re-fetches translations through the loader. reloadTranslations() re-fetches the current locale, which is useful after translations change on the server. Both operations report progress through the global loader.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function TranslationControls() {
    const { t, locale, setLocale, reloadTranslations, ready } = useTranslations();

    if (!ready) {
        return <p>Loading translations…</p>;
    }

    return (
        <section lang={locale}>
            <h1>{t("settings.language.title")}</h1>

            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setLocale("en")}
                disabled={locale === "en"}
            >
                English
            </button>

            <button
                type="button"
                onClick={() => setLocale("nl")}
                disabled={locale === "nl"}
            >
                Nederlands
            </button>

            <button type="button" onClick={reloadTranslations}>
                {t("translations.reload")}
            </button>

            <p>{t("settings.language.current", { locale })}</p>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider loader={loadTranslations} defaultLocale="en">
                <TranslationControls />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I report missing translation keys? ​

Solution: Pass onMissingTranslation to I18nProvider. The callback receives the missing key and locale and is intended for reporting only; it cannot supply a fallback value. Pair it with logging or your monitoring service.

tsx
import { GlobalLoaderProvider, I18nProvider, useTranslations } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { TranslationLoader } from "blendsdk/react";

const loadTranslations: TranslationLoader = async (locale) => {
    const response = await fetch(`/api/translations/${locale}`);
    if (!response.ok) {
        throw new Error(`Translation request failed with ${response.status}`);
    }
    return response.json();
};

function TranslationProbe() {
    const { t } = useTranslations();
    return <p>{t("dashboard.title")}</p>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <GlobalLoaderProvider>
            <I18nProvider
                loader={loadTranslations}
                defaultLocale="en"
                onMissingTranslation={(key, locale) => {
                    console.warn(
                        `Missing translation "${key}" for locale "${locale}"`,
                    );
                }}
            >
                <TranslationProbe />
            </I18nProvider>
        </GlobalLoaderProvider>
    );
}

How do I configure the BFF auth endpoints? ​

Solution: Provide basePath and any optional AuthConfig overrides. The provider merges them with AUTH_DEFAULTS on mount. Endpoint paths are relative to basePath. The resolved values are available through useAuth().config.

SettingDefault
basePathRequired
endpoints.login"/login"
endpoints.callback"/callback"
endpoints.logout"/logout"
endpoints.me"/me"
endpoints.refresh"/refresh"
loginPath"/login"
notAuthorizedPath"/not-authorized"
defaultReturnTo"/"
autoRefreshtrue
refreshLeadTime60
csrfHeader"x-csrf-token"
tsx
import { AUTH_DEFAULTS, AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { AuthConfig } from "blendsdk/react";

const authConfig: AuthConfig = {
    basePath: "/api/auth",
    endpoints: {
        ...AUTH_DEFAULTS.endpoints,
        me: "/session",
        refresh: "/session/refresh",
    },
    loginPath: "/sign-in",
    notAuthorizedPath: "/no-access",
    defaultReturnTo: "/dashboard",
    autoRefresh: true,
    refreshLeadTime: 30,
    csrfHeader: "x-csrf-token",
};

function ResolvedEndpoints() {
    const { config } = useAuth();

    return (
        <ul>
            <li>
                Login endpoint: {config.basePath}
                {config.endpoints.login}
            </li>
            <li>
                Session endpoint: {config.basePath}
                {config.endpoints.me}
            </li>
            <li>
                Refresh endpoint: {config.basePath}
                {config.endpoints.refresh}
            </li>
            <li>Login route: {config.loginPath}</li>
            <li>Not-authorized route: {config.notAuthorizedPath}</li>
            <li>CSRF header: {config.csrfHeader}</li>
        </ul>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={authConfig}>
            <ResolvedEndpoints />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

How do I sign a user in and out? ​

Solution: Use useAuth(). login(returnTo?) navigates the browser to the BFF login endpoint; it is a navigation, not an async function. logout() calls the BFF logout endpoint and clears local state, so await it and handle errors. Check isLoading before treating an absent user as anonymous.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionControls() {
    const { user, isAuthenticated, isLoading, login, logout } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking your session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated || user === null) {
        return (
            <button type="button" onClick={() => login("/dashboard")}>
                Sign in
            </button>
        );
    }

    const handleLogout = async (): Promise<void> => {
        try {
            await logout();
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not sign out", error);
        }
    };

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Signed in as {user.sub}</p>
            <button type="button" onClick={() => void handleLogout()}>
                Sign out
            </button>
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SessionControls />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

How do I protect a route so unauthenticated users are redirected to login? ​

Solution: Wrap the protected route element with AuthGuard, place it inside AuthProvider, and render it inside a router. AuthGuard redirects unauthenticated users to config.loginPath. This scenario requires the optional react-router peer; install it alongside the blendsdk umbrella, react, and react-dom.

tsx
import { AuthGuard, AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";
import { BrowserRouter, Route, Routes } from "react-router";

function LoginPage() {
    const { isAuthenticated, isLoading, login } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking your session…</p>;
    }

    if (isAuthenticated) {
        return <p>You are already signed in.</p>;
    }

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => login()}>
            Sign in
        </button>
    );
}

function DashboardPage() {
    return <h1>Dashboard</h1>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <BrowserRouter>
            <AuthProvider
                config={{
                    basePath: "/api/auth",
                    loginPath: "/login",
                    defaultReturnTo: "/dashboard",
                }}
            >
                <Routes>
                    <Route path="/login" element={<LoginPage />} />
                    <Route
                        path="/dashboard"
                        element={
                            <AuthGuard>
                                <DashboardPage />
                            </AuthGuard>
                        }
                    />
                </Routes>
            </AuthProvider>
        </BrowserRouter>
    );
}

For grant-based gating, RequireAccess applies the same redirect pattern but sends signed-in users without the required grant to config.notAuthorizedPath. Can conditionally renders a UI fragment without redirecting. Both use the same roles and permissions as useAuthorization().

How do I distinguish an authenticated session from an authorized one? ​

Solution: isAuthenticated means a user object exists. authorized is the server's separate decision and is false before the first session check, for anonymous or failed checks, for a session the application denied, and after logout. Check isLoading first, then branch on both flags.

ValueMeaning
userAuthUser or null
isAuthenticateduser !== null
authorizedServer returned a session that is not marked authorized: false
isLoadingInitial session check is in progress
tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function SessionStatus() {
    const { isLoading, isAuthenticated, authorized, user } = useAuth();

    if (isLoading) {
        return <p>Checking session…</p>;
    }

    if (!isAuthenticated || user === null) {
        return <p>No session. Sign in to continue.</p>;
    }

    if (!authorized) {
        return (
            <p>
                Signed in as {user.sub}, but the server has not authorized this
                session.
            </p>
        );
    }

    return <p>Signed in and authorized as {user.sub}.</p>;
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <SessionStatus />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

How do I send the CSRF token with a state-changing request? ​

Solution: Read csrfToken and config.csrfHeader from useAuth(), then add the token as a request header when it is not null. If CSRF is not enforced, the token is null and the header can be omitted. The token is a snapshot; if the server rotates the session token, a request made with an outdated value can be rejected with 403.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuth } from "blendsdk/react";

function DeleteInvoiceButton() {
    const { csrfToken, config, isAuthenticated } = useAuth();

    const remove = async (): Promise<void> => {
        const headers: Record<string, string> = {};

        if (csrfToken !== null) {
            headers[config.csrfHeader] = csrfToken;
        }

        try {
            const response = await fetch("/api/invoices/42", {
                method: "DELETE",
                headers,
            });

            if (!response.ok) {
                throw new Error(`Delete failed with ${response.status}`);
            }
        } catch (error) {
            console.error("Could not delete invoice", error);
        }
    };

    if (!isAuthenticated) {
        return null;
    }

    return (
        <button type="button" onClick={() => void remove()}>
            Delete invoice
        </button>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <DeleteInvoiceButton />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

How do I show UI based on roles and permissions? ​

Solution: Use useAuthorization(), which derives the principal from the session user and exposes roles, permissions, hasRole(), and can(). The values are readonly and the predicates are stable while the user object is unchanged. Authorization is presentation only: the server must enforce the same grants on every endpoint.

tsx
import { AuthProvider, useAuthorization } from "blendsdk/react";

function InvoiceToolbar() {
    const { roles, permissions, hasRole, can } = useAuthorization();

    return (
        <section>
            <p>Roles: {roles.length > 0 ? roles.join(", ") : "none"}</p>
            <p>
                Permissions:{" "}
                {permissions.length > 0 ? permissions.join(", ") : "none"}
            </p>

            {hasRole("finance") && <strong>Finance approval</strong>}

            {can("invoice:write") && (
                <button type="button">Edit invoice</button>
            )}

            {can("invoice:delete") && (
                <button type="button">Delete invoice</button>
            )}
        </section>
    );
}

export function App() {
    return (
        <AuthProvider config={{ basePath: "/api/auth" }}>
            <InvoiceToolbar />
        </AuthProvider>
    );
}

Anonymous users and malformed roles or permissions claims produce an empty principal, so every check returns false instead of throwing. For declarative element gating, Can wraps the same kind of check; for route-level grant gating, RequireAccess redirects to config.notAuthorizedPath.

How do I manage a form with a single object state? ​

Solution: Use useObjectState<T>() with an interface type. The factory runs lazily on mount, setState accepts a partial patch or a functional updater, and reset re-runs the original factory. The setter and reset callbacks are stable across renders. The hook is provider-independent.

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";
import type { FormEvent } from "react";

interface ProfileFormState {
    firstName: string;
    lastName: string;
    age: number;
    newsletter: boolean;
}

export function ProfileForm() {
    const [form, setForm, resetForm] = useObjectState<ProfileFormState>(() => ({
        firstName: "",
        lastName: "",
        age: 0,
        newsletter: false,
    }));

    const submit = (event: FormEvent<HTMLFormElement>): void => {
        event.preventDefault();
        console.log("Submitting profile", form);
    };

    return (
        <form onSubmit={submit}>
            <label>
                First name
                <input
                    value={form.firstName}
                    onChange={(event) =>
                        setForm({ firstName: event.target.value })
                    }
                />
            </label>

            <label>
                Last name
                <input
                    value={form.lastName}
                    onChange={(event) =>
                        setForm({ lastName: event.target.value })
                    }
                />
            </label>

            <label>
                Age
                <input
                    type="number"
                    value={form.age}
                    onChange={(event) => {
                        const age = Number.parseInt(event.target.value, 10);
                        setForm({ age: Number.isNaN(age) ? 0 : age });
                    }}
                />
            </label>

            <label>
                <input
                    type="checkbox"
                    checked={form.newsletter}
                    onChange={(event) =>
                        setForm({ newsletter: event.target.checked })
                    }
                />
                Newsletter
            </label>

            <button type="submit">Save</button>
            <button type="button" onClick={resetForm}>
                Reset
            </button>
        </form>
    );
}

How do I update a nested field or apply two updates in one event? ​

Solution: The merge is shallow. To update a nested object, spread the previous nested value into the patch. To apply multiple updates in the same event, use the functional updater form so each update receives the latest state instead of a stale render value.

tsx
import { useObjectState } from "blendsdk/react";

interface CheckoutState {
    customer: {
        name: string;
        email: string;
    };
    quantity: number;
}

export function CheckoutEditor() {
    const [checkout, setCheckout, resetCheckout] =
        useObjectState<CheckoutState>(() => ({
            customer: { name: "", email: "" },
            quantity: 1,
        }));

    const setEmail = (email: string): void => {
